metadata.title: All-In-One Robust Estimator of the Gaussian Mean

extraction_notes.note: The align holding (ineq:3) and (ineq:4) has two rows with their own left-hand sides but is delivered as one fact; kept as one equation node with the fact's span. (ineq:3) is Koltchinskii-Lounici Th. 4, (ineq:4) is Proposition 2.

Several \Cref targets look wrong: proof of Theorem 2 (and C) cites Lemma 1 (lemma0) and lem:smaxbis where Lemma 2 (geometric median) and Lemma 12 are meant; proof of Lemma 9 cites lem:8 where Lemma 8 (lem:9) is meant. The ref edges are kept and inferred edges to the intended lemmas added. Label eq:L21 is defined twice.

Display (lower) in Section 2 is the same lower bound as Proposition 4 (Appendix D, 'A detailed proof of this claim'); treated as a restated copy in also_stated_at, so the equation has no node of its own.
Lower bound for GAC marked external: the paper attributes it to the theory of Chen-Gao-Ren combined with Bateni-Dalalyan and only spells out the proof.
Subsection 8.1 gives details of one step (eq:3) of the prose proof of Fact 3; extracted as a continuation proof part of Fact 3 with a uses edge to the first part.

Facts are tcolorbox environments labelled f1..f5 but cited as fact:f1..fact:f5 (and Algorithms a1/a2 as algo:a1/algo:a2), so these \Cref keys are unresolved; the edges they state were added by hand (basis named).
Literature results mentioned in Section 4 (Tukey median rate, filtering algorithms, etc.) and the empirical figures of Section 7 are not extracted as nodes.
The Statistician's worst-case-risk minimization is typed problem (it also introduces R_max); definition was the alternative.

nodes.name: Vector norms $\ell_2$, $\ell_1$, $\ell_\infty$
nodes.statement: For any vector $\boldsymbol v$, we use the norm notations $\|\boldsymbol v\|_2$ for the standard Euclidean norm, $\|\boldsymbol v\|_1$ for the sum of absolute values of entries and $\|\boldsymbol v\|_\infty$ for the largest in absolute value entry of $\boldsymbol v$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Tensor square $\boldsymbol v^{\otimes 2}$
nodes.statement: The tensor product of $\boldsymbol v$ by itself is denoted by $\boldsymbol v^{\otimes 2} = \boldsymbol v\boldsymbol v^\top$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Probability simplex and unit sphere
nodes.statement: We denote by $\boldsymbol\Delta^{n-1}$ and by $\mathbb S^{n-1}$, respectively, the probability simplex and the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^n$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Largest eigenvalue and its positive part
nodes.statement: For any symmetric matrix $\mathbf M$, $\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf M)$ is the largest eigenvalue of $\mathbf M$, while $\lambda_{\max,+}(\mathbf M)$ is its positive part.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Operator norm
nodes.statement: The operator norm of $\mathbf M$ is denoted by $\|\mathbf M\|_{\textup{op}}$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Effective rank
nodes.statement: We will often use the effective rank $\mathbf r_{\mathbf M}$ defined as $\mathop{\textup{Tr}}(\mathbf M)/\|\mathbf M\|_{ \textup{op}}$, where $\mathop{\textup{Tr}}(\mathbf M)$ is the trace of matrix $\mathbf M$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Loewner order
nodes.statement: For symmetric matrices $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ of the same size we write $\mathbf A \succeq \mathbf B$, if the matrix $\mathbf A - \mathbf B$ is positive semidefinite.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Extreme singular values
nodes.statement: For a rectangular $p\times n$ matrix $\mathbf A$, we let $s_{\min}(\mathbf A)$ and $s_{\max}(\mathbf A)$ be the smallest and the largest singular values of $\mathbf A$ defined respectively as $s_{\min}(\mathbf A) = \inf_{\boldsymbol v\in\mathbb S^{n-1}} \|\mathbf A\boldsymbol v\|_2$ and $s_{\max}(\mathbf A) = \sup_{\boldsymbol v\in\mathbb S^{n-1}} \|\mathbf A\boldsymbol v\|_2$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Cone of PSD matrices
nodes.statement: The set of all $p\times p$ positive semidefinite matrices is denoted by $\mathcal S_{+}^p$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Gaussian with adversarial contamination (GAC)
nodes.statement: We say that the distribution $\mathbf P\!_n$ of data $\boldsymbol X_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol X_n$ is Gaussian with adversarial contamination, denoted by $\mathbf P\!_n\in \textup{GAC}(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)$ with $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$ and $\boldsymbol\Sigma\succeq 0$, if there is a set of $n$ independent and identically distributed random vectors $\boldsymbol Y_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol Y_n$ drawn from $\mathcal N_p(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma)$ satisfying \begin{align} \big|\{i:\boldsymbol X_i\neq \boldsymbol Y_i \}\big|\le \varepsilon n. \end{align}
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator
nodes.genus: distribution $\mathbf P\!_n$ of data $\boldsymbol X_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol X_n$
differentia: there is a set of $n$ independent and identically distributed random vectors $\boldsymbol Y_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol Y_n$ drawn from $\mathcal N_p(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma)$
nodes.statement_short: Data are GAC if at most $\varepsilon n$ of them differ from an i.i.d. $\mathcal N_p(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma)$ sample.
nodes.label: def:1

nodes.name: Equation (1)
nodes.statement: \big|\{i:\boldsymbol X_i\neq \boldsymbol Y_i \}\big|\le \varepsilon n.
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator

nodes.name: Outliers and inliers
nodes.statement: In what follows, the sample points $\boldsymbol X_i$ with indices in the set $\mathcal O = \{i:\boldsymbol X_i\neq \boldsymbol Y_i\}$ are called outliers, while all the other sample points are called inliers.
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator

nodes.name: Set of inliers $\mathcal I$
nodes.statement: We define $\mathcal I = \{1, \ldots,n\}\setminus\mathcal O$, the set of inliers.
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator

nodes.name: Expected estimation error $R_{\mathbf P\!_n}$
nodes.statement: The Statistician aims at estimating $\boldsymbol\mu^*$ as accurately as possible, the accuracy being measured by the expected estimation error: \begin{align} R_{\mathbf P\!_n}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n, \boldsymbol\mu^*) = \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n - \boldsymbol\mu^*\|_{\mathbb L_2({\mathbf P\!_n})} = \bigg(\sum_{j=1}^p \mathbf E_{\mathbf P\!_n} [(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n-\boldsymbol\mu^*)_j^2]\bigg)^{1/2}. \end{align}
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator

nodes.name: Equation (2)
nodes.statement: R_{\mathbf P\!_n}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n, \boldsymbol\mu^*) = \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n - \boldsymbol\mu^*\|_{\mathbb L_2({\mathbf P\!_n})} = \bigg(\sum_{j=1}^p \mathbf E_{\mathbf P\!_n} [(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n-\boldsymbol\mu^*)_j^2]\bigg)^{1/2}.
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator

nodes.name: Minimax robust mean estimation under adversarial contamination
nodes.statement: The goal of the Statistician is to find an estimator $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n$ that minimizes the worst-case risk \begin{align} R_{\max}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon) = \sup_{\boldsymbol\mu^*\in\mathbb R^p} \sup_{\mathbf P\!_n\in\textup{GAC}(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)} R_{\mathbf P\!_n}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n, \boldsymbol\mu^*). \end{align}
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator
nodes.statement_short: Find an estimator minimizing the worst-case risk $R_{\max}$ over all means and all GAC contaminations.

nodes.name: Equation (3)
nodes.statement: R_{\max}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon) = \sup_{\boldsymbol\mu^*\in\mathbb R^p} \sup_{\mathbf P\!_n\in\textup{GAC}(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)} R_{\mathbf P\!_n}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n, \boldsymbol\mu^*).
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator

nodes.name: Effective rank of $\boldsymbol\Sigma$
nodes.statement: Let $\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma} = \mathop{\textup{Tr}}(\boldsymbol\Sigma)/\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|_{\textup{op}}$ be the effective rank of $\boldsymbol\Sigma$.
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator

nodes.name: Minimax rate optimal estimator
nodes.statement: We say that the estimator $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n$ is minimax rate optimal (in expectation), if there are universal constants $c_1$, $c_2$ and $C$ such that \begin{align} R_{\max}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon) \le C\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|^{1/2}_{\textup{op}} \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}{n}} + \varepsilon\bigg) \end{align} for every $(n,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)$ satisfying $\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}\le c_1 n$ and $\varepsilon\le c_2$.
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator
nodes.statement_short: An estimator is minimax rate optimal if its worst-case risk is at most $C\|\Sigma\|^{1/2}(\sqrt{r_\Sigma/n}+\varepsilon)$ for small $r_\Sigma/n$ and $\varepsilon$.
nodes.label: def:2

nodes.name: Equation (5)
nodes.statement: R_{\max}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon) \le C\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|^{1/2}_{\textup{op}} \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}{n}} + \varepsilon\bigg)
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator

nodes.name: Asymptotically efficient estimator
nodes.statement: We say that $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n$ is an asymptotically efficient estimator of $\boldsymbol\mu^*$, if when $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_n$ tends to zero sufficiently fast, as $n$ tends to infinity, we have \begin{align} R_{\max}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon) \le \|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|^{1/2}_{\textup{op}} \sqrt{\frac{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}{n}}\,\big( 1 + o_n(1)\big). \end{align}
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator
nodes.statement_short: Worst-case risk matches $\|\Sigma\|^{1/2}\sqrt{r_\Sigma/n}$ up to a $1+o(1)$ factor when $\varepsilon_n\to 0$ fast enough.
nodes.label: def:3

nodes.name: Equation (6)
nodes.statement: R_{\max}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon) \le \|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|^{1/2}_{\textup{op}} \sqrt{\frac{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}{n}}\,\big( 1 + o_n(1)\big).
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator

nodes.name: Efficiency of the sample mean without outliers
nodes.statement: We recall here that in the outlier-free situation, the sample mean is asymptotically efficient and its worst-case risk is equal to $\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|^{1/2}_{\textup{op}} \sqrt{{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}/{n}}$.
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator
conclusions: the sample mean is asymptotically efficient and its worst-case risk is equal to $\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|^{1/2}_{\textup{op}} \sqrt{{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}/{n}}$

nodes.name: Necessary condition for asymptotic efficiency
nodes.statement: One can infer from \eqref{lower} that a necessary condition for the existence of asymptotically efficient estimator is $\varepsilon_n^2 = o_n(\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n)$.
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator
conclusions: a necessary condition for the existence of asymptotically efficient estimator is $\varepsilon_n^2 = o_n(\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n)$

nodes.name: Finite-sample breakdown point
nodes.statement: We say that $\varepsilon_n^*\in[0,1/2]$ is the (finite-sample) breakdown point of the estimator $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n$, if \begin{align} R_{\max}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon) < +\infty,\qquad \forall \varepsilon < \varepsilon^*_n \end{align} and $R_{\max}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon) = +\infty$, for every $\varepsilon>\varepsilon^*_n$.
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator
nodes.statement_short: $\varepsilon_n^*$ is the threshold below which the worst-case risk is finite and above which it is infinite.
nodes.label: def:4

nodes.name: Equation (7)
nodes.statement: R_{\max}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon) < +\infty,\qquad \forall \varepsilon < \varepsilon^*_n
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator

nodes.name: Breakdown point of componentwise and geometric medians
nodes.statement: One can check that the breakdown points of the componentwise median and the geometric median (see the definition of $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}}$ in \eqref{GM:def} below) equal $1/2$.
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator
conclusions: the breakdown points of the componentwise median and the geometric median (see the definition of $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}}$ in \eqref{GM:def} below) equal $1/2$

nodes.name: Breakdown point of Tukey's median
nodes.statement: Among all rate-optimal (up to a polylogarithmic factor) robust estimators, Tukey's median is\footnote{Recent results in \citep{zhu2020tukey} suggest that an estimator based on the TV-projection may achieve the optimal breakdown point of $1/2$.} the one with highest known breakdown point equal to $1/3$ \citep{DonGasko}.
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator
conclusions: the one with highest known breakdown point equal to $1/3$

nodes.name: Rate-breakdown point
nodes.statement: We say that $\varepsilon_{r}^*\in[0,1/2]$ is the $r(n,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)$-breakdown point of the estimator $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n$ for a given function $r:\mathbb N\times\mathcal S_{+}^p \times [0,1/2)$, if for every $\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{r}^*$, \begin{align} \sup_{n,p} \frac{R_{\max}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n(\varepsilon),\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)}{r(n, \boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)} < +\infty, \end{align} and $\varepsilon^*_r$ is the largest value satisfying this property.
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator
nodes.statement_short: $\varepsilon_r^*$ is the largest contamination level below which the worst-case risk stays within a constant of the rate $r$.

nodes.name: Equation (8)
nodes.statement: \sup_{n,p} \frac{R_{\max}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n(\varepsilon),\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)}{r(n, \boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)} < +\infty,
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator

nodes.name: Minimax-rate-breakdown point
nodes.statement: In the context of Gaussian mean estimation, if the previous definition is applied with $r(n,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon) = \|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|_{\textup{op}} \big(\sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n} + \varepsilon)$, we call the corresponding value the minimax-rate-breakdown point.
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator

nodes.name: Nearly-minimax-rate-breakdown point
nodes.statement: Similarly, if $r(n,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon) = \|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|_{\textup{op}}\big(\sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n} + \varepsilon \sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)})$, we call the corresponding value the nearly-minimax-rate-breakdown point.
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator

nodes.name: SQ lower bound for robust Gaussian mean estimation
nodes.statement: It should be mentioned here that the extra $\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}$ factor cannot be avoided by any Statistical Query (SQ) polynomial-time algorithm, as shown by the SQ lower bound established in \citep{DiakonikolasKS17}.
nodes.section: 2 Desirable properties of a robust estimator
conclusions: the extra $\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}$ factor cannot be avoided by any Statistical Query (SQ) polynomial-time algorithm

nodes.name: Weighted mean $\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w}$ and cost $G(\boldsymbol w,\boldsymbol\mu)$
nodes.statement: To this end, we set \begin{align} \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i \boldsymbol X_i,\qquad G(\boldsymbol w,\boldsymbol\mu) = \lambda_{\max,+}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu) ^{\otimes 2} - \boldsymbol\Sigma\bigg) \end{align} for any pair of vectors $\boldsymbol w\in[0,1]^n$ and $\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^p$.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Weighted mean of the data and $G$ = positive part of the top eigenvalue of the weighted second moment minus $\Sigma$.

nodes.name: Equation (9)
nodes.statement: \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i \boldsymbol X_i,\qquad G(\boldsymbol w,\boldsymbol\mu) = \lambda_{\max,+}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu) ^{\otimes 2} - \boldsymbol\Sigma\bigg)
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.label: notations1

nodes.name: Ideal weight vector $\boldsymbol w^*$
nodes.statement: The main idea of the proposed methods is to find a weight vector $\widehat{\boldsymbol w}_n$ belonging to the probability simplex \begin{align} \boldsymbol\Delta^{n-1} = \Big\{\boldsymbol w\in [0,1]^n : w_1+\ldots +w_n = 1\Big\} \end{align} that mimics the ideal weight vector $\boldsymbol w^*$ defined by $w^*_j = \mathds 1(j\in\mathcal I)/|\mathcal I|$, so that the weighted average $\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\widehat{\boldsymbol w}_n}$ is nearly as close to $\boldsymbol\mu^*$ as the average of the inliers.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Seek weights in the simplex mimicking the ideal weights $w^*_j = 1(j\in\mathcal I)/|\mathcal I|$ (uniform on inliers).

nodes.name: Equation (10)
nodes.statement: \boldsymbol\Delta^{n-1} = \Big\{\boldsymbol w\in [0,1]^n : w_1+\ldots +w_n = 1\Big\}
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach

nodes.name: Equation (11)
nodes.statement: \sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu)^{\otimes 2} = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\boldsymbol X_i- \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w})^{\otimes 2} + (\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} - \boldsymbol\mu)^{\otimes 2} \succeq \sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\boldsymbol X_i-\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w})^{\otimes 2}.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach

nodes.name: Minimality of $G$ at the weighted mean
nodes.statement: G(\boldsymbol w,\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w}) = \min_{\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^n} G(\boldsymbol w,\boldsymbol\mu),\qquad \forall \boldsymbol w\in\boldsymbol\Delta^{n-1}.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.label: eq:minG

nodes.name: Iteratively reweighted mean estimator (known $\varepsilon$ and $\Sigma$)
nodes.statement: \small \STATE {\bfseries Input:} data $\boldsymbol X_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol X_n\in\mathbb R^p$, contamination rate $\varepsilon$ and $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ \STATE {\bfseries Output:} parameter estimate $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}$ \STATE {\bfseries Initialize:} compute $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^0$ as a minimizer of $\sum_{i=1}^n \|\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu\|_2$\\[7pt] \STATE Set $K = 0\vee\Big\lceil \frac{\log(4\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}) - 2\log(\varepsilon({1-2\varepsilon}))} {2\log(1-2\varepsilon) - \log \varepsilon -\log(1-\varepsilon)} \Big\rceil$.\\[7pt] \STATE {{\bf For} $k=1:K$} \STATE \qquad {Compute current weights:}\\ \qquad\quad $\displaystyle \boldsymbol w \in \mathop{\textup{arg\,min}}_{(n-n\varepsilon)\|\boldsymbol w\|_\infty\le 1} \lambda_{\max}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i (\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}) ^{\otimes 2}- \boldsymbol\Sigma\bigg)\vee 0. $ \STATE \qquad{Update the estimator: $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^k = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i\boldsymbol X_i$}. \STATE {\bfseries EndFor} \STATE {{\bf Return} $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{K}$}.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
input: data $\boldsymbol X_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol X_n\in\mathbb R^p$, contamination rate $\varepsilon$ and $\boldsymbol\Sigma$
nodes.statement_short: Start from the geometric median; repeat $K$ times: solve an SDP for capped weights minimizing the excess top eigenvalue, then take the weighted mean.

nodes.name: Geometric median
nodes.statement: To give a concrete example, and also in order to guarantee equivariance by similarity transformations, we assume that $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^0$ is the geometric median: \begin{align} \widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^0 = \widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}} \in\textup{arg}\min_{\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^p} \sum_{i=1}^n\|\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu\|_2. \end{align}
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: The initial estimator is the geometric median, minimizing the sum of Euclidean distances to the data.

nodes.name: Equation (13)
nodes.statement: \widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^0 = \widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}} \in\textup{arg}\min_{\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^p} \sum_{i=1}^n\|\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu\|_2.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.label: GM:def

nodes.name: Iteratively reweighted mean estimator
nodes.statement: We call iteratively reweighted mean estimator, denoted by $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}$, the $K$-th element of the sequence $\{\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^k; k=0,1,\ldots\}$ starting from $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^0$ in \eqref{GM:def} and defined by the recursion \begin{align} \widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k \in \textup{arg}\min_{(n-n\varepsilon)\|\boldsymbol w\|_\infty\le 1} G(\boldsymbol w,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}),\qquad \widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^k = \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^{k}}, \end{align} where the minimum is over all weight vectors $\boldsymbol w\in\boldsymbol\Delta^{n-1}$ satisfying $\max_j w_j\le 1/(n-n\varepsilon)$ and the number of iteration is \begin{align} K = 0\bigvee \bigg\lceil \frac{\log(4\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}) - 2\log(\varepsilon({1-2\varepsilon}))}{2\log(1-2\varepsilon) - \log \varepsilon -\log(1-\varepsilon)}\bigg\rceil. \end{align}
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Start at the geometric median; for $K$ rounds pick weights (capped at $1/(n-n\varepsilon)$) minimizing $G$ and set the estimate to the weighted mean.
nodes.label: IR:def

nodes.name: IR weight update
nodes.statement: \widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k \in \textup{arg}\min_{(n-n\varepsilon)\|\boldsymbol w\|_\infty\le 1} G(\boldsymbol w,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}),\qquad \widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^k = \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^{k}},
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.label: iter:1

nodes.name: Number of iterations $K$
nodes.statement: K = 0\bigvee \bigg\lceil \frac{\log(4\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}) - 2\log(\varepsilon({1-2\varepsilon}))}{2\log(1-2\varepsilon) - \log \varepsilon -\log(1-\varepsilon)}\bigg\rceil.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.label: K

nodes.name: Choice of the number of iterations $K$
nodes.statement: Note that the value of $K$ provided above is tailored to the case where the initial estimator is the geometric median. Clearly, $K$ depends only logarithmically on the dimension and $K = K_\varepsilon$ tends to 2 when $\varepsilon$ goes to zero, see \Cref{fig:k-eps}. Note also that the choice of $K$ in \eqref{K} is derived from the condition $\big(\sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon) }/(1-2\varepsilon )\big)^K\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^0-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_{\mathbf L_2} \le \varepsilon$, see \eqref{ineq:GMR} below. We can use any other initial estimator of $\boldsymbol\mu^*$ instead of the geometric median, provided that $K$ is large enough to satisfy the last inequality.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: $K$ grows logarithmically in dimension, tends to 2 as $\varepsilon\to0$, and is set so that the initial error is contracted below $\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Computationally tractable estimator
nodes.statement: An estimator is called computationally tractable, if its computational complexity is at most polynomial in $n$, $p$ and $1/\varepsilon$.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach

nodes.name: Computational tractability of the IR estimator
nodes.statement: {}{f1} The estimator $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}$ is computationally tractable.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach

nodes.name: Proof of Fact 1
nodes.statement: In order to check computational tractability, it suffices to prove that each iteration of the algorithm can be performed in polynomial time. Since the number of iterations depends logarithmically on $\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}\le p$, this will suffice. Note now that the optimization problem in \eqref{iter:1} is convex and can be cast into a semi-definite program. Indeed, it is equivalent to minimizing a real value $t$ over all the pairs $(t,\boldsymbol w)$ satisfying the constraints \begin{align} t\ge 0,\quad \boldsymbol w\in\boldsymbol\Delta^{n-1},\quad \|\boldsymbol w\|_\infty\le \frac1{n(1-\varepsilon)},\quad \sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{\otimes 2} \preceq \boldsymbol\Sigma + t\mathbf I_p. \end{align} The first two constraints can be rewritten as a set of linear inequalities, while the third constraint is a linear matrix inequality.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Each iteration is a convex problem castable as an SDP, and the number of iterations is logarithmic.

nodes.name: Reduce to per-iteration complexity
nodes.statement: In order to check computational tractability, it suffices to prove that each iteration of the algorithm can be performed in polynomial time. Since the number of iterations depends logarithmically on $\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}\le p$, this will suffice.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: It suffices that each iteration is polynomial since $K$ is logarithmic.

nodes.name: Cast iteration as SDP
nodes.statement: Note now that the optimization problem in \eqref{iter:1} is convex and can be cast into a semi-definite program. Indeed, it is equivalent to minimizing a real value $t$ over all the pairs $(t,\boldsymbol w)$ satisfying the constraints \begin{align} t\ge 0,\quad \boldsymbol w\in\boldsymbol\Delta^{n-1},\quad \|\boldsymbol w\|_\infty\le \frac1{n(1-\varepsilon)},\quad \sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{\otimes 2} \preceq \boldsymbol\Sigma + t\mathbf I_p. \end{align}
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the weight optimization as minimizing $t$ under linear and LMI constraints.

nodes.name: Equation (16)
nodes.statement: t\ge 0,\quad \boldsymbol w\in\boldsymbol\Delta^{n-1},\quad \|\boldsymbol w\|_\infty\le \frac1{n(1-\varepsilon)},\quad \sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{\otimes 2} \preceq \boldsymbol\Sigma + t\mathbf I_p.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach

nodes.name: Constraints are linear/LMI
nodes.statement: The first two constraints can be rewritten as a set of linear inequalities, while the third constraint is a linear matrix inequality.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Linear inequalities plus one LMI: a semidefinite program.

nodes.name: Equivariance of the IR estimator
nodes.statement: {}{f2} The estimator $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}$ is translation, uniform scaling and orthogonal transformation equivariant.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
conclusions: The estimator $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}$ is translation, uniform scaling and orthogonal transformation equivariant.

nodes.name: Proof of Fact 2
nodes.statement: The equivariance mentioned in this statement should be understood as follows. If we denote by $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{n,X}^{ \textup{IR}}$ the estimator computed for data $\boldsymbol X_1,\ldots, \boldsymbol X_n$, and by $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{n,X'}^{\textup{IR}}$ the one computed for data $\boldsymbol X'_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol X'_n$, with $\boldsymbol X_i' = \boldsymbol a + \lambda\mathbf U \boldsymbol X_i$, where $\boldsymbol a\in\mathbb R^p$, $\lambda>0$ and $\mathbf U$ is a $p\times p$ orthogonal matrix, then $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{n,X'}^{\textup{IR}} = \boldsymbol a + \lambda\mathbf U \widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{n,X}^{\textup{IR}}$. To prove this property, we first note that \begin{align} \min_{\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^p} \sum_{i=1}^n\|\boldsymbol X'_i-\boldsymbol\mu\|_2 = \lambda\min_{\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^p}\sum_{i=1}^n\|\boldsymbol X_i- \lambda^{-1}\mathbf U^\top(\boldsymbol\mu-\boldsymbol a)\|_2. \end{align} This implies that $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{n,X}^{\textup{GM}} = \lambda^{-1}\mathbf U^\top(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{n,X'}^{\textup{GM}} -\boldsymbol a)$, which is equivalent to $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{n,X'}^{\textup{GM}} = \boldsymbol a + \lambda\mathbf U\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{n,X}^{\textup{GM}}$. Therefore, the initial value of the recursion is equivariant. If we add to this the fact that\footnote{We use here the notation $G_X(\boldsymbol w,\boldsymbol\mu)$ to make clear the dependence of $G$ in \eqref{notations1} on $\boldsymbol X_i$s. We also stress that when the estimator is computed for the transformed data $\boldsymbol X_i'$, the matrix $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ is naturally replaced by $\lambda^2\mathbf U\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf U^\top$.} $G_X(\boldsymbol w,\boldsymbol\mu) =\lambda^2 G_{X'}(\boldsymbol w,\boldsymbol a + \lambda\mathbf U\boldsymbol\mu)$ for every $(\boldsymbol w,\boldsymbol\mu)$, we get the equivariance of $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}$.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Show the geometric median initializer is equivariant and $G$ transforms covariantly, so each iterate is equivariant.

nodes.name: Meaning of equivariance
nodes.statement: The equivariance mentioned in this statement should be understood as follows. If we denote by $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{n,X}^{ \textup{IR}}$ the estimator computed for data $\boldsymbol X_1,\ldots, \boldsymbol X_n$, and by $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{n,X'}^{\textup{IR}}$ the one computed for data $\boldsymbol X'_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol X'_n$, with $\boldsymbol X_i' = \boldsymbol a + \lambda\mathbf U \boldsymbol X_i$, where $\boldsymbol a\in\mathbb R^p$, $\lambda>0$ and $\mathbf U$ is a $p\times p$ orthogonal matrix, then $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{n,X'}^{\textup{IR}} = \boldsymbol a + \lambda\mathbf U \widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{n,X}^{\textup{IR}}$.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: State what equivariance means for transformed data $a+\lambda U X_i$.

nodes.name: Equivariance of geometric median
nodes.statement: To prove this property, we first note that \begin{align} \min_{\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^p} \sum_{i=1}^n\|\boldsymbol X'_i-\boldsymbol\mu\|_2 = \lambda\min_{\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^p}\sum_{i=1}^n\|\boldsymbol X_i- \lambda^{-1}\mathbf U^\top(\boldsymbol\mu-\boldsymbol a)\|_2. \end{align} This implies that $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{n,X}^{\textup{GM}} = \lambda^{-1}\mathbf U^\top(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{n,X'}^{\textup{GM}} -\boldsymbol a)$, which is equivalent to $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{n,X'}^{\textup{GM}} = \boldsymbol a + \lambda\mathbf U\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_{n,X}^{\textup{GM}}$. Therefore, the initial value of the recursion is equivariant.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Change variables in the geometric median objective to get its equivariance.

nodes.name: Equation (17)
nodes.statement: \min_{\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^p} \sum_{i=1}^n\|\boldsymbol X'_i-\boldsymbol\mu\|_2 = \lambda\min_{\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^p}\sum_{i=1}^n\|\boldsymbol X_i- \lambda^{-1}\mathbf U^\top(\boldsymbol\mu-\boldsymbol a)\|_2.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach

nodes.name: Covariance of $G$ gives equivariance
nodes.statement: If we add to this the fact that\footnote{We use here the notation $G_X(\boldsymbol w,\boldsymbol\mu)$ to make clear the dependence of $G$ in \eqref{notations1} on $\boldsymbol X_i$s. We also stress that when the estimator is computed for the transformed data $\boldsymbol X_i'$, the matrix $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ is naturally replaced by $\lambda^2\mathbf U\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf U^\top$.} $G_X(\boldsymbol w,\boldsymbol\mu) =\lambda^2 G_{X'}(\boldsymbol w,\boldsymbol a + \lambda\mathbf U\boldsymbol\mu)$ for every $(\boldsymbol w,\boldsymbol\mu)$, we get the equivariance of $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}$.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Since $G$ transforms covariantly, every iterate is equivariant.

nodes.name: Breakdown points of the IR estimator
nodes.statement: {}{f3} The breakdown point $\varepsilon^*_n$ and the nearly-minimax-rate-breakdown point $\varepsilon^*_r$ of $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}$ satisfy, respectively, $\varepsilon^*_n=0.5$ and $\varepsilon^*_r\ge (5-\sqrt{5})/10\approx 0.28$.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach

nodes.name: Mean error bounded by covariance error (building block)
nodes.statement: We prove later in this paper (see \eqref{eq:fund3}) that if $\boldsymbol X_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol X_n$ satisfy {GAC}$(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)$, there is a random variable $\Xi$ depending only on $\boldsymbol\zeta_i = \boldsymbol Y_i-\boldsymbol\mu^*$, $i=1,\ldots,n$, such that \begin{align} \|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 &\le \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}}{1-2\varepsilon}\, G(\boldsymbol w,\boldsymbol\mu)^{1/2} + \Xi,\quad\forall \boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^p, \end{align} for every $\boldsymbol w\in\boldsymbol\Delta^{n-1}$ such that $n(1-\varepsilon)\|\boldsymbol w\|_\infty \le 1$.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
conclusions: there is a random variable $\Xi$ depending only on $\boldsymbol\zeta_i = \boldsymbol Y_i-\boldsymbol\mu^*$, $i=1,\ldots,n$, such that
nodes.statement_short: Under GAC, the weighted-mean error is at most $\alpha_\varepsilon G(w,\mu)^{1/2}$ plus a data-only remainder $\Xi$, for all feasible weights.

nodes.name: Main inequality
nodes.statement: \|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 &\le \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}}{1-2\varepsilon}\, G(\boldsymbol w,\boldsymbol\mu)^{1/2} + \Xi,\quad\forall \boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^p,
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.label: main:ineq

nodes.name: Proof of Fact 3
nodes.statement: To check \Cref{fact:f3}, we set $\alpha_\varepsilon = {\sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}}/{(1-2\varepsilon)}$ and note that\footnote{See \Cref{ssec:6.1} for more detailed explanations.} \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^k - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 = \|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\, G(\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{1/2} + \Xi\\ &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\, G(\boldsymbol w^*,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{1/2} + \Xi\\ &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\, \big(G(\boldsymbol w^*,\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*}) + \|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\|_2^2 \big)^{1/2} + \Xi\\ &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\,\big( G(\boldsymbol w^*,\boldsymbol\mu^*) + \|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\|_2^2\big)^{1/2} + \Xi\\ &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\,\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 + \widetilde\Xi, \end{align} where $\widetilde\Xi = \alpha_{\varepsilon}\,\big(G(\boldsymbol w^*,\boldsymbol\mu^*)^{1/2} + \|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w^*}\|_2\big) + \Xi$. Unfolding this recursion, we get \footnote{Here and in the sequel $\alpha_{\varepsilon}^K$ stands for $K$-th power of $\alpha_{\varepsilon}$.} \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 = \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^K - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}^K\,\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{0} - \boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 + \frac{\widetilde\Xi}{1-\alpha_\varepsilon}. \end{align} The geometric median $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{0} = \widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}}$ having a breakdown point equal to $1/2$, we infer from the last display that the error of the iteratively reweighted estimator remains bounded after altering $\varepsilon$-fraction of data points provided that $\alpha_\varepsilon <1 $. This implies that the breakdown point is at least equal to the solution of the equation $\sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)} =1-2\varepsilon$, which yields $\varepsilon^*\ge (5-\sqrt{5})/10$. Moreover, if $\varepsilon\in[ (5-\sqrt{5})/10, 1/2]$, then the number of iterations $K$ equals zero and the iteratively reweighted mean coincides with the geometric median. Therefore, its breakdown point is $1/2$.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Derive the contraction $\|\mu^k-\mu^*\|\le\alpha_\varepsilon\|\mu^{k-1}-\mu^*\|+\tilde\Xi$; error stays bounded when $\alpha_\varepsilon<1$, i.e. $\varepsilon<(5-\sqrt5)/10$.

nodes.name: One-step contraction
nodes.statement: To check \Cref{fact:f3}, we set $\alpha_\varepsilon = {\sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}}/{(1-2\varepsilon)}$ and note that\footnote{See \Cref{ssec:6.1} for more detailed explanations.} \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^k - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 = \|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\, G(\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{1/2} + \Xi\\ &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\, G(\boldsymbol w^*,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{1/2} + \Xi\\ &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\, \big(G(\boldsymbol w^*,\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*}) + \|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\|_2^2 \big)^{1/2} + \Xi\\ &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\,\big( G(\boldsymbol w^*,\boldsymbol\mu^*) + \|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\|_2^2\big)^{1/2} + \Xi\\ &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\,\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 + \widetilde\Xi, \end{align} where $\widetilde\Xi = \alpha_{\varepsilon}\,\big(G(\boldsymbol w^*,\boldsymbol\mu^*)^{1/2} + \|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w^*}\|_2\big) + \Xi$.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: With $\alpha_\varepsilon$ defined, derive $\|\mu^k-\mu^*\|\le\alpha_\varepsilon\|\mu^{k-1}-\mu^*\|+\tilde\Xi$.

nodes.name: One-step contraction chain
nodes.statement: \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^k - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 = \|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\, G(\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{1/2} + \Xi\\ &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\, G(\boldsymbol w^*,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{1/2} + \Xi\\ &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\, \big(G(\boldsymbol w^*,\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*}) + \|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\|_2^2 \big)^{1/2} + \Xi\\ &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\,\big( G(\boldsymbol w^*,\boldsymbol\mu^*) + \|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\|_2^2\big)^{1/2} + \Xi\\ &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\,\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 + \widetilde\Xi,
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.label: eq:3

nodes.name: Unfold recursion
nodes.statement: Unfolding this recursion, we get \footnote{Here and in the sequel $\alpha_{\varepsilon}^K$ stands for $K$-th power of $\alpha_{\varepsilon}$.} \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 = \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^K - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}^K\,\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{0} - \boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 + \frac{\widetilde\Xi}{1-\alpha_\varepsilon}. \end{align}
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Iterate the contraction $K$ times.

nodes.name: Unfolded recursion
nodes.statement: \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 = \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^K - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}^K\,\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{0} - \boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 + \frac{\widetilde\Xi}{1-\alpha_\varepsilon}.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.label: main:ineq2

nodes.name: Bounded error when $\alpha_\varepsilon<1$
nodes.statement: The geometric median $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{0} = \widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}}$ having a breakdown point equal to $1/2$, we infer from the last display that the error of the iteratively reweighted estimator remains bounded after altering $\varepsilon$-fraction of data points provided that $\alpha_\varepsilon <1 $. This implies that the breakdown point is at least equal to the solution of the equation $\sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)} =1-2\varepsilon$, which yields $\varepsilon^*\ge (5-\sqrt{5})/10$.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: GM has breakdown 1/2, so the error stays bounded when $\alpha_\varepsilon<1$, giving $\varepsilon^*\ge(5-\sqrt5)/10$.

nodes.name: Large $\varepsilon$: $K=0$
nodes.statement: Moreover, if $\varepsilon\in[ (5-\sqrt{5})/10, 1/2]$, then the number of iterations $K$ equals zero and the iteratively reweighted mean coincides with the geometric median. Therefore, its breakdown point is $1/2$.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: For large $\varepsilon$ the estimator is the geometric median, so the breakdown point is $1/2$.

nodes.name: Near minimax rate optimality of the IR estimator
nodes.statement: {}{f4} The estimator $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}$ is nearly minimax rate optimal, in the sense that its worst-case risk is bounded by $C\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|^{1/2} _{\textup{op}}\big(\sqrt{{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}/{n}} + \varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\big)$, where $C$ is a universal constant.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
conclusions: its worst-case risk is bounded by $C\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|^{1/2}_{\textup{op}}\big(\sqrt{{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}/{n}} + \varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\big)$

nodes.name: Proof of Fact 4
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we assume that $\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|_{\textup{op}}=1$ so that $\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma} = \mathop{\textup{Tr}}(\boldsymbol\Sigma)$. We can always reduce the initial problem to this case by considering scaled data points $\boldsymbol X_i/\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|_{\textup{op}}^{1/2}$ instead of $\boldsymbol X_i$. Combining \eqref{main:ineq2} and the triangle inequality, we get \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_{\mathbb L_2} &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}^K\,\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}} - \boldsymbol\mu^*\|_{\mathbb L_2} + \frac{\|\widetilde\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}}{1-\alpha_\varepsilon}. \end{align} It is not hard to check that $\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}} - \boldsymbol\mu^*\|_{\mathbb L_2}\le 2\sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}/(1-2\varepsilon)$, see \Cref{lem:8} below. Furthermore, the choice of $K$ in \eqref{K} entails $2\alpha_\varepsilon^K\sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}} \le \varepsilon(1-2\varepsilon)$. This implies that \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_{\mathbb L_2} &\le \varepsilon + \frac{\|\widetilde\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}}{1 - \alpha_\varepsilon}. \end{align} The last two building blocks of the proof are the following\footnote{Inequality \eqref{ineq:3} is \citep[Th. 4]{KoltchLounici}, while \eqref{ineq:4} is the claim of \Cref{proposition2} below.} inequalities: \begin{align} &\mathbf E[G(\boldsymbol w^*,\boldsymbol\mu^*)] \le C\big(1 + \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n}\big)\sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n}, \\ &\|\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2} \le \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n}(1+ C\sqrt{\varepsilon}) + C\sqrt{\varepsilon}(\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n)^{1/4} + C\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}, \end{align} where $C>0$ is a universal constant. In what follows, the value of $C$ may change from one line to the other. We have \begin{align} \|\widetilde\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2} &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\big(\|G(\boldsymbol w^*,\boldsymbol\mu^*)^{1/2} \|_{\mathbb L_2} + \|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w^*}\|_{\mathbb L_2}\big) + \|\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}\\ &\le C\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\big(\mathbf E^{1/2}[G(\boldsymbol w^*,\boldsymbol\mu^*)] + \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n}\big) + \|\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}^2\\ &\le C\varepsilon\,\big((\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n)^{1/4} + \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n} \big) + \|\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}\\ &\le \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n}(1+ C\sqrt{\varepsilon}) + C\sqrt{\varepsilon}(\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n)^{1/4} + C\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\\ &\le C\sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n} + C\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}. \end{align} Returning to \eqref{main:ineq2} and combining it with \eqref{ineq:5}, we get the claim of \Cref{fact:f4} for every $\varepsilon\le \varepsilon_0$, where $\varepsilon_0$ is any positive number strictly smaller than $(5-\sqrt{5})/10$. This also proves the second claim of \Cref{fact:f3}.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Unfold the contraction, bound the geometric median error and the remainder $\Xi$ via the Koltchinskii-Lounici bound and Proposition 2.

nodes.name: Normalize $\|\Sigma\|_{op}=1$
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we assume that $\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|_{\textup{op}}=1$ so that $\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma} = \mathop{\textup{Tr}}(\boldsymbol\Sigma)$. We can always reduce the initial problem to this case by considering scaled data points $\boldsymbol X_i/\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|_{\textup{op}}^{1/2}$ instead of $\boldsymbol X_i$.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: WLOG rescale the data so that $\|\Sigma\|_{op}=1$.

nodes.name: $L_2$ version of unfolded bound
nodes.statement: Combining \eqref{main:ineq2} and the triangle inequality, we get \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_{\mathbb L_2} &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}^K\,\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}} - \boldsymbol\mu^*\|_{\mathbb L_2} + \frac{\|\widetilde\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}}{1-\alpha_\varepsilon}. \end{align}
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Take $L_2$ norms in the unfolded recursion.

nodes.name: Unfolded recursion in $L_2$
nodes.statement: \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_{\mathbb L_2} &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}^K\,\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}} - \boldsymbol\mu^*\|_{\mathbb L_2} + \frac{\|\widetilde\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}}{1-\alpha_\varepsilon}.

nodes.label: ineq:GMR

nodes.name: Initial error contracted below $\varepsilon$
nodes.statement: It is not hard to check that $\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}} - \boldsymbol\mu^*\|_{\mathbb L_2}\le 2\sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}/(1-2\varepsilon)$, see \Cref{lem:8} below. Furthermore, the choice of $K$ in \eqref{K} entails $2\alpha_\varepsilon^K\sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}} \le \varepsilon(1-2\varepsilon)$. This implies that \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_{\mathbb L_2} &\le \varepsilon + \frac{\|\widetilde\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}}{1 - \alpha_\varepsilon}. \end{align}
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2 bounds the GM error and the choice of $K$ makes its contribution at most $\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Equation (26)
nodes.statement: \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_{\mathbb L_2} &\le \varepsilon + \frac{\|\widetilde\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}}{1 - \alpha_\varepsilon}.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach

nodes.name: Two building-block inequalities
nodes.statement: The last two building blocks of the proof are the following\footnote{Inequality \eqref{ineq:3} is \citep[Th. 4]{KoltchLounici}, while \eqref{ineq:4} is the claim of \Cref{proposition2} below.} inequalities: \begin{align} &\mathbf E[G(\boldsymbol w^*,\boldsymbol\mu^*)] \le C\big(1 + \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n}\big)\sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n}, \\ &\|\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2} \le \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n}(1+ C\sqrt{\varepsilon}) + C\sqrt{\varepsilon}(\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n)^{1/4} + C\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}, \end{align} where $C>0$ is a universal constant. In what follows, the value of $C$ may change from one line to the other.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Invoke bounds on $E[G(w^*,\mu^*)]$ (Koltchinskii-Lounici) and on $\|\Xi\|_{L_2}$ (Proposition 2).

nodes.name: Building-block inequalities (ineq:3), (ineq:4)
nodes.statement: &\mathbf E[G(\boldsymbol w^*,\boldsymbol\mu^*)] \le C\big(1 + \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n}\big)\sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n},\\ &\|\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2} \le \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n}(1+ C\sqrt{\varepsilon}) + C\sqrt{\varepsilon}(\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n)^{1/4} + C\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)},
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.label: ineq:3

nodes.name: Bound $\|\tilde\Xi\|_{L_2}$
nodes.statement: We have \begin{align} \|\widetilde\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2} &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\big(\|G(\boldsymbol w^*,\boldsymbol\mu^*)^{1/2} \|_{\mathbb L_2} + \|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w^*}\|_{\mathbb L_2}\big) + \|\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}\\ &\le C\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\big(\mathbf E^{1/2}[G(\boldsymbol w^*,\boldsymbol\mu^*)] + \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n}\big) + \|\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}^2\\ &\le C\varepsilon\,\big((\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n)^{1/4} + \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n} \big) + \|\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}\\ &\le \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n}(1+ C\sqrt{\varepsilon}) + C\sqrt{\varepsilon}(\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n)^{1/4} + C\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\\ &\le C\sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n} + C\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}. \end{align}
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Combine the building blocks to bound $\|\tilde\Xi\|_{L_2}$.

nodes.name: Bound on $\|\tilde\Xi\|_{L_2}$
nodes.statement: \|\widetilde\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2} &\le \alpha_{\varepsilon}\big(\|G(\boldsymbol w^*,\boldsymbol\mu^*)^{1/2} \|_{\mathbb L_2} + \|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w^*}\|_{\mathbb L_2}\big) + \|\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}\\ &\le C\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\big(\mathbf E^{1/2}[G(\boldsymbol w^*,\boldsymbol\mu^*)] + \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n}\big) + \|\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}^2\\ &\le C\varepsilon\,\big((\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n)^{1/4} + \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n} \big) + \|\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}\\ &\le \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n}(1+ C\sqrt{\varepsilon}) + C\sqrt{\varepsilon}(\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n)^{1/4} + C\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\\ &\le C\sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n} + C\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.label: ineq:5

nodes.name: Conclude Fact 4
nodes.statement: Returning to \eqref{main:ineq2} and combining it with \eqref{ineq:5}, we get the claim of \Cref{fact:f4} for every $\varepsilon\le \varepsilon_0$, where $\varepsilon_0$ is any positive number strictly smaller than $(5-\sqrt{5})/10$. This also proves the second claim of \Cref{fact:f3}.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Plug into the unfolded recursion to obtain the rate, also giving the rate-breakdown point.

nodes.name: Asymptotic efficiency of the IR estimator
nodes.statement: {}{f5} In the setting $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_n\to 0$ so that $\varepsilon^2\log(1/\varepsilon) = o_n(\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n)$ when $n\to\infty$, the estimator $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}$ is asymptotically efficient.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach

nodes.name: Proof of Fact 5
nodes.statement: The proof of this fact follows from \eqref{main:ineq2} and \eqref{ineq:4}. Indeed, if $\varepsilon^2\log(1/\varepsilon) = o_n(\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n)$, \eqref{ineq:4} implies that \begin{align} \|\widetilde\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}^2 &\le \frac{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}{n}\big(1+ o_n(1)\big). \end{align} Injecting this bound in \eqref{main:ineq2} and using the fact that $\varepsilon$ tends to zero, we get the claim of \Cref{fact:f5}.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Plug the bound on $\|\Xi\|$ from (ineq:4) into the unfolded recursion; with $\varepsilon\to0$ the leading constant is 1.

nodes.name: Ingredients
nodes.statement: The proof of this fact follows from \eqref{main:ineq2} and \eqref{ineq:4}.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: The proof combines (main:ineq2) and (ineq:4).

nodes.name: Remainder is $\sqrt{r_\Sigma/n}(1+o(1))$
nodes.statement: Indeed, if $\varepsilon^2\log(1/\varepsilon) = o_n(\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n)$, \eqref{ineq:4} implies that \begin{align} \|\widetilde\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}^2 &\le \frac{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}{n}\big(1+ o_n(1)\big). \end{align}

nodes.statement_short: Under the rate condition, $\|\tilde\Xi\|^2\le(r_\Sigma/n)(1+o(1))$.

nodes.name: Equation (34)
nodes.statement: \|\widetilde\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2}^2 &\le \frac{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}{n}\big(1+ o_n(1)\big).

nodes.name: Conclude efficiency
nodes.statement: Injecting this bound in \eqref{main:ineq2} and using the fact that $\varepsilon$ tends to zero, we get the claim of \Cref{fact:f5}.
nodes.section: 3 Iterative reweighting approach
nodes.statement_short: Since $\alpha_\varepsilon\to0$, the risk is $\sqrt{r_\Sigma/n}(1+o(1))$.

nodes.name: Robustness to optimization error
nodes.statement: A potentially useful observation, from a computational standpoint, is that it is sufficient to solve the optimization problem in \Cref{iter:1} up to an error proportional to $\sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n} + \sqrt{\varepsilon}$. Indeed, one can easily repeat all the steps in \eqref{eq:3} to check that this optimization error does not alter the order of magnitude of the statistical error.
nodes.section: 4 Relation to prior work and discussion
nodes.statement_short: Solving the weight optimization only up to error of order $\sqrt{r_\Sigma/n}+\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ does not change the statistical rate.

nodes.name: Restricted weight vector $\boldsymbol w_I$
nodes.statement: Let $\boldsymbol w\in\boldsymbol\Delta^{n-1}$ be a vector of weights and let $I$ be a subset of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. We use the notation $\boldsymbol w_{I}$ for the vector obtained from $\boldsymbol w$ by zeroing all the entries having indices outside $I$.
nodes.section: 5 Formal statement of main building blocks

nodes.name: Conditional weight vector $\boldsymbol w_{|I}$
nodes.statement: Considering $\boldsymbol w$ as a probability on $\{1,\ldots, n\}$, we define $\boldsymbol w_{|I}$ as the corresponding conditional probability on $I$ that is \begin{align} \boldsymbol w_{|I}\in \boldsymbol\Delta^{n-1},\qquad (\boldsymbol w_{|I})_i = (w_i/ \|\boldsymbol w_{I}\|_1) \mathds 1(i\in I). \end{align}
nodes.section: 5 Formal statement of main building blocks

nodes.name: Equation (35)
nodes.statement: \boldsymbol w_{|I}\in \boldsymbol\Delta^{n-1},\qquad (\boldsymbol w_{|I})_i = (w_i/ \|\boldsymbol w_{I}\|_1) \mathds 1(i\in I).
nodes.section: 5 Formal statement of main building blocks

nodes.name: Weighted averages $\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w}$, $\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}_{\boldsymbol w_{|I}}$, $\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|I}}$
nodes.statement: We will make repeated use of the notation \begin{align} \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i \boldsymbol X_i,\qquad \bar{\boldsymbol\xi}_{\boldsymbol w_{|I}} = \sum_{i\in I} (\boldsymbol w_{|I})_i \boldsymbol\xi_i,\qquad \bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|I}} = \sum_{i\in I} (\boldsymbol w_{|I})_i \boldsymbol\zeta_i. \end{align}
nodes.section: 5 Formal statement of main building blocks

nodes.name: Equation (36)
nodes.statement: \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i \boldsymbol X_i,\qquad \bar{\boldsymbol\xi}_{\boldsymbol w_{|I}} = \sum_{i\in I} (\boldsymbol w_{|I})_i \boldsymbol\xi_i,\qquad \bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|I}} = \sum_{i\in I} (\boldsymbol w_{|I})_i \boldsymbol\zeta_i.
nodes.section: 5 Formal statement of main building blocks

nodes.name: Mean error controlled by covariance error
nodes.statement: Let $\boldsymbol\zeta_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol\zeta_n$ be a set of vectors such that $\boldsymbol\zeta_i = \boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu^*$ for every $i\in \mathcal I$, where $\mathcal I$ is a subset of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. For every weight vector $\boldsymbol w\in \boldsymbol \Delta^{n-1}$ such that $\sum_{i\not\in \mathcal I} w_i\le \varepsilon_{w}\le 1/2$ and for every $p\times p$ matrix $\boldsymbol\Sigma$, it holds \begin{align} \|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 &\le \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{w}}}{1-\varepsilon_{w}}\, \lambda_{\max,+}^{1/2}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\boldsymbol X_i - \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w})^{\otimes 2} - \boldsymbol\Sigma\Big) + R(\boldsymbol\zeta,\boldsymbol w,\mathcal I), \end{align} with the remainder term \begin{align} R(\boldsymbol\zeta,\boldsymbol w,\mathcal I) = 2\sqrt{\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|_{\rm op}}\varepsilon_{w}+\sqrt{2\varepsilon_{w}}\, \lambda_{\max,+}^{1/2} \bigg(\sum_{i\in \mathcal I} (\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I})_i (\boldsymbol\Sigma - \boldsymbol\zeta_i\boldsymbol\zeta_i^\top)\bigg) + (1+\sqrt{2\varepsilon_{w}}) \|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I}}\|_2. \end{align}

nodes.statement_short: The weighted-mean error is at most $\sqrt{\varepsilon_w}/(1-\varepsilon_w)$ times the root of the excess top eigenvalue of the weighted covariance, plus a remainder $R$ depending on inliers only.

nodes.name: Structure of the capped simplex $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$
nodes.statement: For any integer $\ell>0$, let $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ be the set of all $\boldsymbol w\in\boldsymbol\Delta^{n-1}$ such that $\max_i w_i\le 1/\ell$. The following facts hold: \vspace{-10pt} \begin{enumerate} \item[\textup{ i)}] For every $J\subset \{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that $|J|\ge \ell$, the uniform weight vector $\boldsymbol u^{J}\in \mathcal W_{n,\ell}$. \item[\textup{ ii)}] The set $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ is the convex hull of the uniform weight vectors $\{\boldsymbol u^{J} : |J| = \ell\}$. \item[\textup{ iii)}] For every convex mapping $G:\boldsymbol\Delta^{n-1}\to\mathbb R$, we have \begin{align} \sup_{\boldsymbol w\in \mathcal W_{n,\ell}} G(\boldsymbol w) = \max_{|J| =\ell} G(\boldsymbol u^J), \end{align} where the last maximum is over all subsets $J$ of cardinality $\ell$ of the set $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. \item[\textup{ iv)}] If $\boldsymbol w\in\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ then for any $I$ such that $|I|\ge \ell'>n-\ell$, we have $\boldsymbol w_{|I}\in \mathcal W_{n,\ell+\ell'-n}$. \end{enumerate} \vspace{-10pt}
nodes.section: 5 Formal statement of main building blocks
conclusions: For every $J\subset \{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that $|J|\ge \ell$, the uniform weight vector $\boldsymbol u^{J}\in \mathcal W_{n,\ell}$.
The set $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ is the convex hull of the uniform weight vectors $\{\boldsymbol u^{J} : |J| = \ell\}$.

nodes.statement_short: Weights capped at $1/\ell$ form the convex hull of uniform weights on $\ell$-subsets; convex functions peak at those vertices; conditioning keeps a cap.
nodes.label: lemma0

nodes.name: Feasible weight set $\mathcal W_n(\varepsilon)$
nodes.statement: Let us denote by $\mathcal W_n(\varepsilon)$ the set $\mathcal W_{n,n(1-\varepsilon)}$.

nodes.name: Outlier weight bound on $\mathcal W_n(\varepsilon)$
nodes.statement: It is clear that for $\boldsymbol w\in \mathcal W_n(\varepsilon)$ and for $| I^c|\le n\varepsilon$, we have $\sum_{i\not\in I} w_i\le \varepsilon/(1-\varepsilon)$.

nodes.name: Fundamental inequality for feasible weights
nodes.statement: We now infer from \Cref{proposition1} and \eqref{eq:minG} that \begin{align} \|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_\varepsilon\,\lambda_{\max,+}^{1/2} \Big(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\boldsymbol X_i - \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w}) ^{\otimes 2} - \boldsymbol\Sigma\Big) + \Xi\\ & = \alpha_\varepsilon\, \inf_{\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^p}G(\boldsymbol w, \boldsymbol\mu)^{1/2} + \Xi, \end{align} with $\Xi$ being the largest value of $R(\boldsymbol\zeta,\boldsymbol w, I)$ over all possible weights $\boldsymbol w\in \mathcal W_n(\varepsilon)$ and subsets $I\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}$ satisfying $| I^c|\le n\varepsilon$.
nodes.section: 5 Formal statement of main building blocks
conclusions: \|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_\varepsilon\,\lambda_{\max,+}^{1/2} \Big(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\boldsymbol X_i - \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w}) ^{\otimes 2} - \boldsymbol\Sigma\Big) + \Xi\\ & = \alpha_\varepsilon\, \inf_{\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^p}G(\boldsymbol w, \boldsymbol\mu)^{1/2} + \Xi,
nodes.statement_short: For feasible weights, the weighted-mean error is at most $\alpha_\varepsilon\inf_\mu G(w,\mu)^{1/2}+\Xi$, with $\Xi$ the worst remainder.

nodes.name: Fundamental inequality (eq:fund3)
nodes.statement: \|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} - {\boldsymbol\mu}^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_\varepsilon\,\lambda_{\max,+}^{1/2} \Big(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\boldsymbol X_i - \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w}) ^{\otimes 2} - \boldsymbol\Sigma\Big) + \Xi\\ & = \alpha_\varepsilon\, \inf_{\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^p}G(\boldsymbol w, \boldsymbol\mu)^{1/2} + \Xi,
nodes.section: 5 Formal statement of main building blocks

nodes.name: Bound on the remainder term $\Xi$
nodes.statement: Let $R(\boldsymbol\zeta,\boldsymbol w, I)$ be defined in \Cref{proposition1} and $\boldsymbol\zeta_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol\zeta_n$ be i.i.d. centered Gaussian random vectors with covariance matrix $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ satisfying $\lambda_{\max}(\boldsymbol\Sigma) = 1$. If $\varepsilon\le 0.28$, then the random variable \begin{align} \Xi = \sup_{\boldsymbol w\in \mathcal W_n(\varepsilon)} \max_{|I|\ge n(1-\varepsilon)} R(\boldsymbol\zeta,\boldsymbol w, I) \end{align} satisfies, for a universal constant $C>0$, the inequalities \begin{align} \|\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2} &\le \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n}(1+ C \sqrt{\varepsilon}) + C\sqrt{\varepsilon}(\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n)^{1/4} + C\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)} \\ \|\Xi\|_{\mathbb L_2} &\le \sqrt{p/n}(1+ 16\sqrt{\varepsilon}) + 5\sqrt{3\varepsilon}\,(p/n)^{1/4} + 32\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(2/\varepsilon)}, \end{align} where for the second inequality we assumed that $p\ge 2$ and $n\ge p\vee 4$.

assumptions: $\boldsymbol\zeta_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol\zeta_n$ be i.i.d. centered Gaussian random vectors with covariance matrix $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ satisfying $\lambda_{\max}(\boldsymbol\Sigma) = 1$
for the second inequality we assumed that $p\ge 2$ and $n\ge p\vee 4$

nodes.label: proposition2

nodes.name: Expected-risk bound for the IR estimator
nodes.statement: Let $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}$ be the iteratively reweighted mean defined in~\Cref{IR:def} and Algorithm~\ref{algo:a1}. There is a universal constant $C>0$ such that for any $n,p\ge 1 $ and for every $\varepsilon < (5-\sqrt{5})/10$, we have \begin{align} \sup_{\boldsymbol\mu^*\in\mathbb R^p} \sup_{\mathbf P\!_n\in\textup{GAC}(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)} \mathbf E^{1/2}[\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2^2] \le \frac{C\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|^{1/2}_{\textup{op}}}{1 - 2\varepsilon - \sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}}\, \big(\sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n} + \varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/ \varepsilon)}\big), \end{align} where $\mathbf P\!_n\in\textup{GAC}(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)$ means that the data points $\boldsymbol X_i$ are Gaussian with adversarial contamination, see \Cref{def:1}. If, in addition, $p\ge 2$ and $n\ge p\vee 10$, then \begin{align} \sup_{\boldsymbol\mu^*\in\mathbb R^p} \sup_{\mathbf P\!_n\in\textup{GAC}(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)} \mathbf E^{1/2}[\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2^2] \le \frac{10\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|^{1/2}_{\textup{op}}}{1-2\varepsilon - \sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}}\, \big(\sqrt{p/n} + \varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\big). \end{align}
nodes.section: 5 Formal statement of main building blocks
assumptions: $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}$ be the iteratively reweighted mean defined in~\Cref{IR:def} and Algorithm~\ref{algo:a1}
nodes.statement_short: The IR estimator's worst-case root-mean-square error is $\lesssim\|\Sigma\|^{1/2}(\sqrt{r_\Sigma/n}+\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)})/(1-2\varepsilon-\sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)})$; constant 10 for $n\ge p\vee10$.
nodes.label: th:1
