nodes.name: Sub-Gaussian random vector
nodes.statement: Recall that a zero-mean random vector $\boldsymbol\xi$ is called sub-Gaussian with parameter $\tau>0$ (also known as the variance proxy), if \begin{align} \mathbf E[e^{\boldsymbol v^\top\boldsymbol\xi}] \le e^{\nicefrac{\tau}2 \|\boldsymbol v\|_2^2},\qquad \forall \boldsymbol v\in\mathbb R^p. \end{align}
nodes.section: 6.1 High-probability risk bound for a sub-Gaussian reference distribution

nodes.name: Equation (47)
nodes.statement: \mathbf E[e^{\boldsymbol v^\top\boldsymbol\xi}] \le e^{\nicefrac{\tau}2 \|\boldsymbol v\|_2^2},\qquad \forall \boldsymbol v\in\mathbb R^p.
nodes.section: 6.1 High-probability risk bound for a sub-Gaussian reference distribution

nodes.name: Notation $SG_p(\tau)$
nodes.statement: We write $\boldsymbol\xi \sim SG_p(\tau)$.
nodes.section: 6.1 High-probability risk bound for a sub-Gaussian reference distribution

nodes.name: Standard Gaussian is sub-Gaussian
nodes.statement: If $\boldsymbol\xi$ is standard Gaussian then it is sub-Gaussian with parameter $1$.
nodes.section: 6.1 High-probability risk bound for a sub-Gaussian reference distribution

nodes.name: Bounded centered vectors are sub-Gaussian
nodes.statement: Similarly, if $\boldsymbol\xi$ is centered and belongs almost surely to the unit ball, then $\boldsymbol\xi$ is sub-Gaussian with parameter 1.
nodes.section: 6.1 High-probability risk bound for a sub-Gaussian reference distribution
assumptions: $\boldsymbol\xi$ is centered and belongs almost surely to the unit ball

nodes.name: Sub-Gaussian model with adversarial contamination (SGAC)
nodes.statement: We say that the joint distribution $\mathbf P\!_n$ of the random vectors $\boldsymbol X_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol X_n\in\mathbb{R}^p$ belongs to the sub-Gaussian model with adversarial contamination with mean $\boldsymbol\mu^*$, covariance matrix $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ and contamination rate $\varepsilon$, if there are independent random vectors $\boldsymbol\xi_i\sim SG_p(\tau)$ such that \begin{align} \Big|\Big\{i:=1,\ldots,n:\boldsymbol X_i \neq \boldsymbol\mu^*+ \boldsymbol\Sigma^{1/2} \boldsymbol\xi_i\Big\}\Big|\le \varepsilon n. \end{align} We then write $\mathbf P\!_n\in \textup{SGAC}(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma, \varepsilon)$.
nodes.section: 6.1 High-probability risk bound for a sub-Gaussian reference distribution
nodes.statement_short: Data are SGAC if all but $\varepsilon n$ points equal $\mu^*+\Sigma^{1/2}\xi_i$ with independent $SG_p(\tau)$ vectors $\xi_i$.
nodes.label: def:SGAC

nodes.name: Equation (48)
nodes.statement: \Big|\Big\{i:=1,\ldots,n:\boldsymbol X_i \neq \boldsymbol\mu^*+ \boldsymbol\Sigma^{1/2} \boldsymbol\xi_i\Big\}\Big|\le \varepsilon n.
nodes.section: 6.1 High-probability risk bound for a sub-Gaussian reference distribution

nodes.name: GAC is a special case of SGAC
nodes.statement: It is clear that a Gaussian model with adversarial contamination defined in \Cref{def:1} is a particular case of the sub-Gaussian model with adversarial contamination. In other terms, the set \textup{SGAC}$(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)$ is strictly larger than the set \textup{GAC}$(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)$.
nodes.section: 6.1 High-probability risk bound for a sub-Gaussian reference distribution
conclusions: a Gaussian model with adversarial contamination defined in \Cref{def:1} is a particular case of the sub-Gaussian model with adversarial contamination

nodes.name: High-probability bound for the IR estimator under SGAC
nodes.statement: Let $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}$ be the iteratively reweighted mean defined in~\Cref{IR:def} and in Algorithm~\ref{algo:a1}. Let $\delta\in(4e^{-n},1)$ be a tolerance level. There exists a constant $A_5$ depending only on the variance proxy $\tau$ such that if $n\ge p\ge 2$ and $\varepsilon < (5-\sqrt{5})/10$, then for every $\boldsymbol\mu^*\in\mathbb R^p$ and every $\mathbf P\!_n\in\textup{SGAC}(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)$, we have \begin{align} \mathbf P\Bigg(\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2^2 \le \frac{A_5\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|^{1/2}_{\textup{op}}}{1-2 \varepsilon - \sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}}\, \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{p+\log(4/\delta)}{n}} + \varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\bigg)\Bigg) \le 1 - 4\delta. \end{align}
nodes.section: 6.1 High-probability risk bound for a sub-Gaussian reference distribution
assumptions: $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}$ be the iteratively reweighted mean defined in~\Cref{IR:def} and in Algorithm~\ref{algo:a1}
nodes.statement_short: Under sub-Gaussian adversarial contamination, with probability $\ge1-4\delta$ the IR error is $\lesssim\sqrt{(p+\log(4/\delta))/n}+\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}$.
nodes.label: th:2

nodes.name: Equation (49)
nodes.statement: \mathbf P\Bigg(\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2^2 \le \frac{A_5\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|^{1/2}_{\textup{op}}}{1-2 \varepsilon - \sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}}\, \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{p+\log(4/\delta)}{n}} + \varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\bigg)\Bigg) \le 1 - 4\delta.
nodes.section: 6.1 High-probability risk bound for a sub-Gaussian reference distribution

nodes.name: Optimality of the rate for sub-Gaussian distributions
nodes.statement: Let us just mention that \cite[Section 1.2]{Chengetal19} claim that the rate $\sqrt{p/n} + \varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/ \varepsilon)}$ is optimal for sub-Gaussian distributions, meaning that, unlike the Gaussian case, the $\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}$ factor cannot be removed.
nodes.section: 6.1 High-probability risk bound for a sub-Gaussian reference distribution
conclusions: the rate $\sqrt{p/n} + \varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/ \varepsilon)}$ is optimal for sub-Gaussian distributions

nodes.name: Euclidean ball $\mathbb B(\boldsymbol\mu,r)$
nodes.statement: We will denote by $\mathbb B(\boldsymbol\mu,r)$ the ball with center $\boldsymbol\mu$ and radius $r$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb R^p$.
nodes.section: 6.2 Adaptation to unknown contamination rate $\varepsilon$

nodes.name: Adaptively chosen iteratively reweighted mean (Lepski's method)
nodes.statement: We choose a geometric grid $\varepsilon_\ell = a^\ell \varepsilon_0$, $\ell = 1,2,\ldots,\ell_{\max}$, of possible values of the contamination rate. Here, $a\in(0,1)$ is a real number, $\varepsilon_0 = (5-\sqrt{5})/10$ and $\ell_{\max} = [0.5\log_a (p/n)]$. For each $\ell=1,\ldots, \ell_{\max}$, we denote by $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}( \varepsilon_\ell)$ the iteratively reweighted mean computed for $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_\ell$, see Algorithm~\ref{algo:a1}, and we set \begin{align} R_\delta(z) = \frac{A_5\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|^{1/2}_{\textup{op}}} {1-2z - \sqrt{z(1-z)}}\, \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{p+\log(4\ell_{\max}/\delta)}{n}} + z\sqrt{\log(1/z)}\bigg), \qquad z\in[0, \varepsilon_0), \end{align} where $\delta\in(0,1)$ is a tolerance level and $A_5$ is the constant from \Cref{th:2}. The adaptively chosen iteratively reweighted mean estimator $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{AIR}}$ is defined by $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{AIR}} = \widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}} (\varepsilon_{\widehat\ell})$ where \begin{align} \widehat\ell = \max\Big\{\ell\le \ell_{\max} : \bigcap_{j=1}^\ell \mathbb B\big(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}} (\varepsilon_j);R_\delta(\varepsilon_j)\big)\neq \varnothing\Big\}. \end{align}
nodes.section: 6.2 Adaptation to unknown contamination rate $\varepsilon$
nodes.statement_short: Run IR on a geometric grid of contamination levels and pick the largest index whose confidence balls all intersect (Lepski's method).
nodes.label: def:AIR

nodes.name: Equation (50)
nodes.statement: R_\delta(z) = \frac{A_5\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|^{1/2}_{\textup{op}}} {1-2z - \sqrt{z(1-z)}}\, \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{p+\log(4\ell_{\max}/\delta)}{n}} + z\sqrt{\log(1/z)}\bigg), \qquad z\in[0, \varepsilon_0),
nodes.section: 6.2 Adaptation to unknown contamination rate $\varepsilon$

nodes.name: Equation (51)
nodes.statement: \widehat\ell = \max\Big\{\ell\le \ell_{\max} : \bigcap_{j=1}^\ell \mathbb B\big(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}} (\varepsilon_j);R_\delta(\varepsilon_j)\big)\neq \varnothing\Big\}.
nodes.section: 6.2 Adaptation to unknown contamination rate $\varepsilon$

nodes.name: Computability of the adaptive estimator
nodes.statement: The estimator $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{AIR}}$ can be computed without the knowledge of the true contamination rate $\varepsilon$. Furthermore, its computational complexity nearly of the same order as the complexity of computing a single instance of the iteratively reweighted mean as defined by Algorithm~\ref{algo:a1}. Indeed, to compute $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{AIR}}$, one needs to apply Algorithm~\ref{algo:a1} at most $\ell_{\max} = [0.5 \log_a (p/n)]$ times, and to solve a second-order cone program for checking whether the intersection of a small number of balls is empty.
nodes.section: 6.2 Adaptation to unknown contamination rate $\varepsilon$
nodes.statement_short: AIR needs no knowledge of $\varepsilon$ and costs at most $\ell_{\max}$ IR runs plus an SOCP feasibility check.

nodes.name: Adaptation to unknown contamination rate
nodes.statement: Let $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{AIR}}$ be the estimator defined in~\Cref{def:AIR}. Let $\delta\in(4e^{-n},1)$ be a tolerance level. Let $n\ge p\ge 2$ and $\varepsilon \le (5-\sqrt{5})a/10$, where $a\in(0,1)$ is the parameter used in \Cref{def:AIR}. Then, for every $\boldsymbol\mu^*\in\mathbb R^p$ and every $\mathbf P\!_n\in\textup{SGAC}(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)$, we have \begin{align} \mathbf P\Bigg(\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{AIR}}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2^2 \le \frac{3A_5\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|^{1/2}_{\textup{op}}}{a-2 \varepsilon - \sqrt{\varepsilon(a-\varepsilon)}}\, \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{p+\log(4\ell_{\max}/\delta)}{n}} + \varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\bigg)\Bigg) \le 1 - 4\delta. \end{align}
nodes.section: 6.2 Adaptation to unknown contamination rate $\varepsilon$
assumptions: $n\ge p\ge 2$ and $\varepsilon \le (5-\sqrt{5})a/10$, where $a\in(0,1)$ is the parameter used in \Cref{def:AIR}
nodes.statement_short: Without knowing $\varepsilon$, the Lepski-type AIR estimator attains the IR high-probability rate up to a factor 3.
nodes.label: th:3

nodes.name: Equation (52)
nodes.statement: \mathbf P\Bigg(\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{AIR}}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2^2 \le \frac{3A_5\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|^{1/2}_{\textup{op}}}{a-2 \varepsilon - \sqrt{\varepsilon(a-\varepsilon)}}\, \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{p+\log(4\ell_{\max}/\delta)}{n}} + \varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\bigg)\Bigg) \le 1 - 4\delta.
nodes.section: 6.2 Adaptation to unknown contamination rate $\varepsilon$

nodes.name: Breakdown point of the adaptive estimator
nodes.statement: The breakdown point of the adaptive estimator $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^ {\textup{AIR}}$ inferred from the last theorem is slightly smaller than the one of $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}$. Indeed, there is a factor $a<1$ between these two quantities. Note that one can choose $a$ to be very close to one. The only drawback of choosing $a$ too close to one is the higher computational complexity of the resulting estimator.
nodes.section: 6.2 Adaptation to unknown contamination rate $\varepsilon$

nodes.name: Iteratively reweighted mean estimator (known $\varepsilon$, unknown $\Sigma$)
nodes.statement: \small \STATE {\bfseries Input:} data $\boldsymbol X_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol X_n\in\mathbb R^p$, contamination rate $\varepsilon$ \STATE {\bfseries Output:} parameter estimate $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}$ \STATE {\bfseries Initialize:} compute $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^0$ as a minimizer of $\sum_{i=1}^n \|\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu\|_2$\\[7pt] \STATE Set $K = 0\vee\Big\lceil \frac{\log(4p) - 2\log(\varepsilon({1-2\varepsilon}))} {2\log(1-2\varepsilon) - \log \varepsilon -\log(1-\varepsilon)} \Big\rceil$.\\[7pt] \STATE {{\bf For} $k=1:K$} \STATE \qquad {Compute current weights:}\\ \qquad\quad $\displaystyle \boldsymbol w \in \mathop{\textup{arg\,min}}_{(n-n\varepsilon)\|\boldsymbol w\|_\infty\le 1} \lambda_{\max}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i (\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}) ^{\otimes 2}\bigg). $ \STATE \qquad{Update the estimator: $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^k = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i\boldsymbol X_i$}. \STATE {\bfseries EndFor} \STATE {{\bf Return} $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{K}$}.
nodes.section: 6.2 Adaptation to unknown contamination rate $\varepsilon$
input: data $\boldsymbol X_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol X_n\in\mathbb R^p$, contamination rate $\varepsilon$
nodes.statement_short: Same as Algorithm 1 but minimizes the top eigenvalue of the uncentered weighted second moment, without $\Sigma$.

nodes.name: Argument for the isotropic case
nodes.statement: The first situation is when the covariance matrix is isotropic, $\boldsymbol\Sigma = \sigma^2\mathbf I_p$, with unknown $\sigma>0$. One can easily check that all the claims of \Cref{sec:method} and \Cref{sec:formal} hold true for a slight modification of $\widehat\mu_n^{\textup{IR}}$ obtained by minimizing $\lambda_{\max}(\sum_i w_i(\boldsymbol X_i -\widehat\mu^{k-1})^{\otimes 2}-\boldsymbol\Sigma)$ instead of $G(\boldsymbol w,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})$ in \eqref{iter:1}. For isotropic matrices $\boldsymbol\Sigma$, we have \begin{align} \text{arg}\min_{\boldsymbol w}\lambda_{\max}\bigg (\sum_i w_i(\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat\mu^{k-1})^{\otimes 2}-\sigma^2 \mathbf I_p\bigg) = \text{arg}\min_{\boldsymbol w}\lambda_{\max}\bigg (\sum_i w_i(\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat\mu^{k-1})^{\otimes 2}\bigg), \end{align} which means that the resulting value is independent of $\boldsymbol\Sigma$.

nodes.statement: One can check that \begin{align} \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^* (\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{\otimes 2} &= \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^*(\boldsymbol X_i-\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*})^{\otimes 2} + (\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{\otimes 2}\\ &\preceq \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^*(\boldsymbol X_i-\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*})^{\otimes 2} + \big\|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\big\|_2^2\,\mathbf I_p\\ &\preceq \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^*(\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu^*)^{\otimes 2} + \big\|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\big\|_2^2\,\mathbf I_p. \end{align} This readily yields \begin{align} G(\boldsymbol w^*,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}) &\le \lambda_{\max,+}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^*(\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu^*)^{\otimes 2} - \boldsymbol\Sigma\bigg) + \big\|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\big\|_2^2\\ &\le G(\boldsymbol w^*, \boldsymbol\mu^*) + \big(\big\|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w^*}\big\|_2 + \big\|\boldsymbol\mu^*-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\big\|_2\big)^2. \end{align} To get the last line of \eqref{eq:3}, it suffices to apply the elementary consequence of the Minkowskii inequality $\sqrt{a+ (b+c)^2} \le \sqrt{a+b^2} + c$, for every $a,b,c>0$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Recall that the geometric median of $\boldsymbol X_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol X_n$ is defined by \begin{align} \widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}} \in\textup{arg}\min_{\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^p} \sum_{i=1}^n\|\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu\|_2. \end{align} It is clear that \begin{align} \sum_{i=1}^n\|\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}}\|_2 &\le \sum_{i=1}^n\|\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 \end{align} Without loss of generality, we assume that $\boldsymbol\mu^*= \mathbf 0$. We also assume that $n\varepsilon$ is an integer. On the one hand, we have the simple bound \begin{align} n(1-\varepsilon)\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}}\|_2 &\le \sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\big(\|\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}}\|_2 + \|\boldsymbol\zeta_i\|_2\big)\\ &\le \sum_{i=1}^n\|\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}}\|_2 + \sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\|\boldsymbol\zeta_i\|_2 -\sum_{i\in\mathcal O}\|\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}}\|_2\\ &\le \sum_{i=1}^n\|\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 + \sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\|\boldsymbol\zeta_i\|_2 -\sum_{i\in\mathcal O}\|\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}}\|_2\\ &\le 2\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\|\boldsymbol\zeta_i\|_2 +\sum_{i\in\mathcal O}\big(\|\boldsymbol X_i\|_2-\|\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}}\|_2\big)\\ &\le 2\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\|\boldsymbol\zeta_i\|_2 +n\varepsilon \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}}\|_2, \end{align} where the first and the last inequalities follow from triangle inequality. From the last display, we infer that \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{GM}}\|_{\mathbb L_2} &\le \frac{2}{n(1-2\varepsilon)} \sum_{i=1}^n \|\boldsymbol\zeta_i\|_{\mathbb L_2} \le \frac{2}{1-2\varepsilon} \|\boldsymbol\zeta_1\|_{\mathbb L_2} \le \frac{2\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}^{1/2}}{1-2\varepsilon} \end{align} and we get the claim of the lemma.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: To ease notation throughout this proof, we write $\bar\varepsilon$ instead of $\varepsilon_{w}$. Simple algebra yields \begin{align} \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} - \boldsymbol\mu^* - \bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{\mathcal I}} &= \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w_{\mathcal I}} + \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w_{\mathcal I^c}} - \boldsymbol\mu^* - \bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{\mathcal I}} \\ & = (1-\bar\varepsilon)\boldsymbol\mu^* + \bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{\mathcal I}} + \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w_{\mathcal I^c}} - \boldsymbol\mu^* - \bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{\mathcal I}}\\ & = \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w_{\mathcal I^c}} - \bar\varepsilon\boldsymbol\mu^*\\ & = \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w_{\mathcal I^c}} - \bar\varepsilon\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} + \bar\varepsilon(\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} - \boldsymbol\mu^* ). \end{align} This implies that $(1-\bar\varepsilon)(\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} - \boldsymbol\mu^*) - \bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{\mathcal I}} = \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w_{\mathcal I^c}} - \bar\varepsilon\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w}$, which is equivalent to \begin{align} \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} - \boldsymbol\mu^* - \bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I}} = \frac{\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w_{\mathcal I^c}} - \bar\varepsilon\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w}} {1-\bar\varepsilon}. \end{align} Therefore, we have \begin{align} \big\|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} - \boldsymbol\mu^* - \bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I}}\big\|_2 & = \frac{\big\|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w_{\mathcal I^c}} - \bar\varepsilon\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w}\big\|_2}{1-\bar\varepsilon}\\ & = \frac1{1-\bar\varepsilon} \bigg\|\sum_{i\in\mathcal I^c} w_i(\boldsymbol X_i - \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w})\bigg\|_2\\ & = \frac1{1-\bar\varepsilon} \sup_{\boldsymbol v\in\mathbb S^{p-1}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal I^c} w_i\,\boldsymbol v^\top(\boldsymbol X_i - \bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w}). \end{align} Using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality as well as the notations $\mathbf M_i = (\boldsymbol X_i-\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w})^{\otimes 2}$ and $\mathbf M = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i\mathbf M_i$, we get \begin{align} \bigg\{\sum_{i\in\mathcal I^c} w_i\,\boldsymbol v^\top(\boldsymbol X_i-\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w})\bigg\}^2 &\le \sum_{i\in\mathcal I^c} w_i\sum_{i\in\mathcal I^c} w_i| \boldsymbol v^\top(\boldsymbol X_i-\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w})|^2 =\bar\varepsilon\, \boldsymbol v^\top\sum_{i\in\mathcal I^c} w_i\mathbf{M}_i\boldsymbol v\\ &=\bar\varepsilon\,\boldsymbol v^\top\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\mathbf{M}_i\boldsymbol v- \boldsymbol v^\top\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} w_i\mathbf{M}_i\boldsymbol v\\ &={\bar\varepsilon}\,\boldsymbol v^\top\big(\mathbf{M} - \boldsymbol\Sigma\big)\boldsymbol v + {\bar\varepsilon}\boldsymbol v^\top\Big(\boldsymbol\Sigma-\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} w_i \mathbf{M}_i\Big)\boldsymbol v\\ &\le \bar\varepsilon\,\lambda_{\max}\big( \mathbf{M}-\boldsymbol\Sigma\big) + \bar\varepsilon\,\Big\{\boldsymbol v^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma\boldsymbol v - \boldsymbol v^\top\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} w_i\mathbf{M}_i\boldsymbol v\Big\}. \end{align} Finally, for any unit vector $\boldsymbol v$, \begin{align} \boldsymbol v^\top\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} w_i\mathbf{M}_i \boldsymbol v &= (1-\bar\varepsilon) \,\boldsymbol v^\top\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} (\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I})_i(\boldsymbol X_i-\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w})^{\otimes 2}\boldsymbol v\\ &\ge(1-\bar\varepsilon)\,\boldsymbol v^\top\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} (\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I})_i (\boldsymbol X_i-\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I}})^{\otimes 2}\boldsymbol v\\ & = (1-\bar\varepsilon)\,\boldsymbol v^\top\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} (\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I})_i (\boldsymbol\zeta_i-\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I}})^{\otimes 2}\boldsymbol v\\ &= (1-\bar\varepsilon)\,\boldsymbol v^\top\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} (\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I})_i \boldsymbol\zeta_i\boldsymbol\zeta_i^\top\boldsymbol v-(1-\bar\varepsilon)\, (\boldsymbol v^\top\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I}})^2\\ &\ge (1 -\bar\varepsilon)\bigg(\boldsymbol v^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma\boldsymbol v - \lambda_{\max} \bigg(\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} (\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I})_i (\boldsymbol\Sigma- \boldsymbol\zeta_i\boldsymbol\zeta_i^\top)\bigg) - \|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I}}\|_2^2 \bigg). \end{align} Combining \eqref{eq:p12} and \eqref{eq:p13}, we get \begin{align} \bigg\{\sum_{i\in\mathcal I^c} w_i\,\boldsymbol v^\top(\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu)\bigg\}^2 &\le \bar\varepsilon\,\lambda_{\max}\big( \mathbf{M}-\boldsymbol\Sigma\big) + \bar\varepsilon^2\,\lambda_{\max}\big(\boldsymbol\Sigma\big) \\ &\qquad +\bar\varepsilon(1-\bar\varepsilon)\bigg\{ \lambda_{\max} \bigg(\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} (\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I})_i(\boldsymbol\Sigma - \boldsymbol\zeta_i\boldsymbol\zeta_i^\top)\bigg) + \|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I}}\|_2^2 \bigg\}. \end{align} In conjunction with \eqref{eq:p11b}, this yields \begin{align} \big\|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} - \boldsymbol\mu^* - \bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I}}\big\|_2 & \leq \frac{\sqrt{\bar\varepsilon}}{1-\bar\varepsilon} \bigg( \lambda_{\max}\big( \mathbf{M}-\boldsymbol\Sigma\big) + \bar\varepsilon\,\lambda_{\max}\big(\boldsymbol\Sigma\big) \\ &\qquad +(1-\bar\varepsilon)\bigg\{ \lambda_{\max} \bigg(\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} (\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I})_i(\boldsymbol\Sigma - \boldsymbol\zeta_i\boldsymbol\zeta_i^\top)\bigg) + \|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|\mathcal I}}\|_2^2 \bigg\}\bigg)^{1/2}. \end{align} From this relation, using the triangle inequality and the inequality $\sqrt{a_1+\ldots + a_n}\le \sqrt{a_1}+\ldots+\sqrt{a_n}$, we get \begin{align} \big\|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w} - nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Claim i) of this lemma is straightforward. For ii), we use the fact that the compact convex polytope $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ is the convex hull of its extreme points. The fact that each uniform weight vector $\boldsymbol u^{J}$ is an extreme point of $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ is easy to check. Indeed, if for two points $\boldsymbol w$ and $\boldsymbol w'$ from $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ we have $\boldsymbol u^{J} = 0.5(\boldsymbol w+\boldsymbol w')$, then we necessarily have $\boldsymbol w_{J^c} = \boldsymbol w'_{J^c} = 0$. Therefore, for any $j\in J$, \begin{align} \frac1{\ell} \ge w_j = 1 - \sum_{i\in J\setminus\{j\}} w_i \ge 1-\big(\ell-1)\times \frac1{\ell}=\frac1{\ell}. \end{align} This implies that $w_j=\frac1{\ell}\mathds 1(j\in J)$. Hence, $\boldsymbol w = \boldsymbol u^{J}$ and the same is true for $\boldsymbol w'$. Hence, $\boldsymbol u^{J}$ is an extreme point. Let us prove now that all the extreme points of $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ are of the form $\boldsymbol u^{J}$ with $|J| = \ell$. Let $\boldsymbol w\in \mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ be such that one of its coordinates is strictly positive and strictly smaller than $1/\ell$. Without loss of generality, we assume that the two smallest nonzero entries of $\boldsymbol w$ are $w_1$ and $w_2$. We have $0<w_1<1/\ell$ and $0<w_2<1/\ell$. Set $\rho = w_1\wedge w_2 \wedge \{1/\ell - w_1\}\wedge \{1/\ell - w_2\}$. For $\boldsymbol w^+ = \boldsymbol w + (\rho,-\rho,0,\ldots,0)$ and $\boldsymbol w^- = \boldsymbol w - (\rho,-\rho, 0,\ldots,0)$, we have $\boldsymbol w^+,\boldsymbol w^-\in\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ and $\boldsymbol w = 0.5(\boldsymbol w^++\boldsymbol w^-)$. Therefore, $\boldsymbol w$ is not an extreme point of $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$. This completes the proof of ii). Claim ii) implies that $\mathcal W_{n,\ell} = \{\sum_{|J|=\ell} \alpha_J \boldsymbol u^J: \boldsymbol\alpha \in \boldsymbol\Delta^{K-1}\}$ with $K={n\choose \ell}$. Hence, \begin{align} \sup_{\boldsymbol w\in \mathcal W_{n,\ell}} G(\boldsymbol w) &= \sup_{\boldsymbol\alpha\in\boldsymbol\Delta^{K-1}} G\bigg(\sum_{|J|=\ell} \alpha_J \boldsymbol u^J\bigg) \le \sup_{\boldsymbol\alpha\in\boldsymbol\Delta^{K-1}} \sum_{|J|=\ell} \alpha_J G\big(\boldsymbol u^J\big) \le \max_{|J| =\ell} G(\boldsymbol u^J) \end{align} and claim iii) follows. To prove iv), we check that \begin{align} \|\boldsymbol w_{ I}\|_1 = \sum_{i\in I} w_i = 1 - \sum_{i\not\in I} w_i \ge 1-\frac{| I^c|}{\ell} \ge 1- \frac{n-\ell'}{\ell} = \frac{\ell+\ell'-n}{\ell}. \end{align} This readily yields $(\boldsymbol w_{|I})_i \le 1/(\ell+\ell'-n)$, which leads to the claim of item iv).

Let us prove now that all the extreme points of $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ are of the form $\boldsymbol u^{J}$ with $|J| = \ell$. Let $\boldsymbol w\in \mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ be such that one of its coordinates is strictly positive and strictly smaller than $1/\ell$. Without loss of generality, we assume that the two smallest nonzero entries of $\boldsymbol w$ are $w_1$ and $w_2$. We have $0<w_1<1/\ell$ and $0<w_2<1/\ell$. Set $\rho = w_1\wedge w_2 \wedge \{1/\ell - w_1\}\wedge \{1/\ell - w_2\}$. For $\boldsymbol w^+ = \boldsymbol w + (\rho,-\rho,0,\ldots,0)$ and $\boldsymbol w^- = \boldsymbol w - (\rho,-\rho, 0,\ldots,0)$, we have $\boldsymbol w^+,\boldsymbol w^-\in\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ and $\boldsymbol w = 0.5(\boldsymbol w^++\boldsymbol w^-)$. Therefore, $\boldsymbol w$ is not an extreme point of $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$. This completes the proof of ii).
nodes.section: 8.4 Proof of 1
nodes.statement_short: Extreme points of $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ are exactly uniform weights on $\ell$-subsets.

nodes.name: Krein-Milman reduction
nodes.statement: For ii), we use the fact that the compact convex polytope $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ is the convex hull of its extreme points.
nodes.section: 8.4 Proof of 1
nodes.statement_short: A compact convex polytope is the hull of its extreme points.

nodes.name: Uniform weights are extreme
nodes.statement: The fact that each uniform weight vector $\boldsymbol u^{J}$ is an extreme point of $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ is easy to check. Indeed, if for two points $\boldsymbol w$ and $\boldsymbol w'$ from $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$ we have $\boldsymbol u^{J} = 0.5(\boldsymbol w+\boldsymbol w')$, then we necessarily have $\boldsymbol w_{J^c} = \boldsymbol w'_{J^c} = 0$. Therefore, for any $j\in J$, \begin{align} \frac1{\ell} \ge w_j = 1 - \sum_{i\in J\setminus\{j\}} w_i \ge 1-\big(\ell-1)\times \frac1{\ell}=\frac1{\ell}. \end{align} This implies that $w_j=\frac1{\ell}\mathds 1(j\in J)$. Hence, $\boldsymbol w = \boldsymbol u^{J}$ and the same is true for $\boldsymbol w'$. Hence, $\boldsymbol u^{J}$ is an extreme point.
nodes.section: 8.4 Proof of 1
nodes.statement_short: If $u^J$ is a midpoint, both points vanish off $J$ and equal $1/\ell$ on $J$.

Therefore, $\boldsymbol w$ is not an extreme point of $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$. This completes the proof of ii).

nodes.statement_short: A weight with a fractional coordinate is a midpoint of two feasible weights.

nodes.statement: Therefore, $\boldsymbol w$ is not an extreme point of $\mathcal W_{n,\ell}$. This completes the proof of ii).

nodes.name: Claim iii): convexity
nodes.statement: Claim ii) implies that $\mathcal W_{n,\ell} = \{\sum_{|J|=\ell} \alpha_J \boldsymbol u^J: \boldsymbol\alpha \in \boldsymbol\Delta^{K-1}\}$ with $K={n\choose \ell}$. Hence, \begin{align} \sup_{\boldsymbol w\in \mathcal W_{n,\ell}} G(\boldsymbol w) &= \sup_{\boldsymbol\alpha\in\boldsymbol\Delta^{K-1}} G\bigg(\sum_{|J|=\ell} \alpha_J \boldsymbol u^J\bigg) \le \sup_{\boldsymbol\alpha\in\boldsymbol\Delta^{K-1}} \sum_{|J|=\ell} \alpha_J G\big(\boldsymbol u^J\big) \le \max_{|J| =\ell} G(\boldsymbol u^J) \end{align} and claim iii) follows.

nodes.statement_short: Write $w$ as a convex combination of $u^J$ and use convexity of $G$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement:
The bias-variance decomposition, in conjunction with \Cref{lem:vershynin}, yields  egin{align} \mathbf E ig[s_{\max}^2( oldsymbol\zeta_{1:n}) ig] &= 	extbf{Var} ig(s_{\max}( oldsymbol\zeta_{1:n}) ig) +\mathbf E ig[s_{\max}( oldsymbol\zeta_{1:n}) ig]^2\ &\le 	extbf{Var} ig(s_{\max}( oldsymbol\zeta_{1:n}) ig)+  ig(\sqrt{n} + \sqrt{	extbf{	extup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle oldsymbol\Sigma}} ig)^2. \end{align} Applying the well-known fact $\mathbf E[Z^2] = \int_0^\infty \mathbf P(Z^2\ge t)\,dt$ to the random variable $Z= s_{\max}( oldsymbol\zeta_{1:n}) - \mathbf E[s_{\max}( oldsymbol\zeta_{1:n})]$ and using the Gaussian concentration inequality, we get  egin{align} 	extbf{Var} ig(s_{\max}( oldsymbol\zeta_{1:n}) ig) &= \int_0^\infty \mathbf{P} \Big( ig|s_{\max}( oldsymbol\zeta_{1:n}) - \mathbf E[s_{\max}( oldsymbol\zeta_{1:n})]  ig|\ge \sqrt{t}\Big)\,dt \le 2\int_0^\infty e^{-t/2}\,dt = 4. \end{align} This completes the proof of \eqref{esp:1}. For every random variable $Z$ and every constant $a>0$, we have  egin{align} \mathbf E ig[((a + Z)^2 - n)_+ ig] &= \mathbf E ig[(a^2+2aZ +Z^2-n)_+ ig] \ &\le \mathbf E ig[(a^2+2aZ-n)_+ ig] + \mathbf E[Z^2]\ &\le |a^2-n| + 2a\mathbf E[Z_+] + \mathbf E[Z^2]. \end{align} Taking $a = \mathbf E[s_{\max}( oldsymbol\zeta_{1:n})]$ and $Z = s_{\max}( oldsymbol\zeta_{1:n}) -\mathbf E[s_{\max}( oldsymbol\zeta_{1:n})]$, we get  egin{align} \mathbf E ig[(s_{\max}( oldsymbol\zeta_{1:n})^2-n)_+ ig] &\le |(\sqrt{n} + \sqrt{	extbf{	extup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle oldsymbol\Sigma}})^2-n| + (\sqrt{n} + \sqrt{	extbf{	extup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle oldsymbol\Sigma}}) \sqrt{2\pi} + 4\ &= 2\sqrt{n	extbf{	extup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle oldsymbol\Sigma}} +	extbf{	extup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle oldsymbol\Sigma} + (\sqrt{n} + \sqrt{	extbf{	extup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle oldsymbol\Sigma}}) \sqrt{2\pi} + 4\ &\le 6\sqrt{n	extbf{	extup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle oldsymbol\Sigma}} + 4	extbf{	extup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle oldsymbol\Sigma},\qquad  orall n\ge 8. \end{align} Similarly, we have  egin{align} \mathbf E ig[( n - (a + Z)^2 )_+ ig] &= \mathbf E ig[(n- a^2 - 2aZ - Z^2)_+ ig] \le (n- a^2)_+ +2a\mathbf E ig[ Z_- ig]. \end{align} Taking $a = \mathbf E[s_{\min}( oldsymbol\xi_{1:n})]$ and $Z = s_{\min}( oldsymbol\xi_{1:n}) -\mathbf E[s_{\min}( oldsymbol\xi_{1:n})]$, we get  egin{align} \mathbf E ig[(n-s_{\min}( oldsymbol\xi_{1:n})^2)_+ ig] &\le (n- \mathbf E[s_{\min}( oldsymbol\xi_{1:n})]^2)_+ +\mathbf E[s_{\min}( oldsymbol\xi_{1:n})] \sqrt{2\pi}\ &\le (n- (\sqrt{n} - \sqrt{p})^2)_++ (\sqrt{n} + \sqrt{p})\sqrt{2\pi}\ &\le 2\sqrt{np} +(\sqrt{n} + \sqrt{p})\sqrt{2\pi}\le 6\sqrt{np}. \end{align} Thus, we have checked \eqref{esp:1b} and \eqref{esp:1c}. In view of \Cref{lem:vershynin}, for every $t>0$,  egin{align} \mathbf P\Big(s_{\max} ig( oldsymbol\zeta_{ ar J} ig) < \sqrt{|\vbox to 7pt{\hbox{$ ar J$}}|} + \sqrt{	extbf{	extup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle oldsymbol\Sigma}}+ t\Big) \ge 1-e^{-t^2/2}. \end{align} Let $I_0\subset [n]$ be any set of cardinality $m$. Combining the relation $\mathbf E[Z] = \int_0^\infty \mathbf P(Z\ge s)\,ds$, the union bound, and \eqref{eq:L33b}, we arrive at  egin{align} \mathbf E\Big[\max_{| ar J| = m} s_{\max}( oldsymbol\zeta_{ ar J})\Big] &\le \sqrt{m}+\sqrt{	extbf{	extup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle oldsymbol\Sigma}}+ \mathbf E\Big[\max_{| ar J| = m}  ig(s_{\max}( oldsymbol\zeta_{ ar J}) - \sqrt{m} - \sqrt{	extbf{	extup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle oldsymbol\Sigma}} ig)_+\Big]\ & = \sqrt{m} + \sqrt{	extbf{	extup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle oldsymbol\Sigma}}+ \int_0^\infty \mathbf P\Big(\max_{| ar J| = m} s_{\max}( oldsymbol\zeta_{ ar J})\ge \sqrt{m} +\sqrt{	extbf{	extup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle oldsymbol\Sigma}} + t \Big)\,dt\ &\le \sqrt{m}+\sqrt{	extbf{	extup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle oldsymbol\Sigma}}+ \int_0^\infty 1 igwedge {n\choose{m}} \mathbf P\Big(s_{\max}( oldsymbol\zeta_{I_0}) \ge \sqrt{m} +\sqrt{	extbf{	extup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle oldsymbol\Sigma}} + t \Big)\,dt\ &\le \sqrt{m} + \sqrt{	extbf{	extup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle oldsymbol\Sigma}} + \int_{0}^\infty  igg\{1 igwedge {n \choose {m}}e^{-t^2/2}  igg\}\,dt. \end{align} From now on, we assume that $m\in [2,n-1]$, which implies that $ {n \choose {m}} \ge n$. Let $t_0$ be the value of $t$ for which the two terms in the last minimum coincide, that is  egin{align} {n \choose{m}}e^{-t_0^2/2} = 1 \quad&\Longleftrightarrow\quad t_0^2 = 2\log{n \choose{m}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad  egin{cases} t_0^2 \le 2m \log(
icefrac{ne}{m}),\ t_0^2 \ge 2 \log(
icefrac{n(n-1)}{2}), \end{cases} \end{align} We have, for $m\ge 1$,  egin{align} \int_{0}^\infty  igg\{1 igwedge {n \choose{m}}e^{-t^2/2}  igg\}\,dt & = t_0 + {n \choose{m}}\int_{t_0}^\infty e^{-t^2/2}\,dt \le {t_0} + {n \choose{m}}  rac{e^{-t^2_0/2}}{t_0}\ & \le {t_0} +  rac{1}{t_0} \le 1.81\sqrt{m \log(
icefrac{ne}{m})}. \end{align} Inequalities \eqref{eq:L35} and \eqref{eq:L37a'} yield  egin{align} \mathbf E\Big[\max_{| ar J| = m}s_{\max} ig( oldsymbol\zeta_{ ar J} ig)\Big] &\le \sqrt{m} + \sqrt{	extbf{	extup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle oldsymbol\Sigma}} + 1.81\sqrt{m \log(
icefrac{ne}{m})}. \end{align} On the other hand, the mapping $ oldsymbol\zeta_{1:n}\mapsto F( oldsymbol\zeta_{1:n}) : = \max_{| ar J| = m}s_{\max} ig( oldsymbol\zeta_{ ar J} ig)$ being 1-Lipschitz, the Gaussian concentration inequality leads to  egin{align} 	extbf{Var} \Big(\max_{| ar J| = m}s_{\max} ig( oldsymbol\zeta_{ ar J} ig)\Big) & = \int_0^\infty 	extbf{P} \Big( ig|F( oldsymbol\zeta_{1:n})-\mathbf E [F( oldsymbol\zeta_{1:n})] ig|\ge\sqrt{t}\Big)\,dt\le 2\int_0^\infty e^{-t/2}\,dt = 4. \end{align} This completes the proof of the lemma.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: Throughout this proof, $\sup_{\boldsymbol w,I}$ stands for the supremum over all $\boldsymbol w\in\mathcal W_n(\varepsilon)$ and over all $I\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}$ of cardinality larger than or equal to $n(1-\varepsilon)$. We recall that, $\Xi = \sup_{\boldsymbol w,I} R(\boldsymbol\zeta, \boldsymbol w,I)$ where for any subset $I$ of$\{1,\ldots,n\}$, \begin{align} R(\boldsymbol\zeta,\boldsymbol w, I) &= 2\varepsilon_{w}+\sqrt{2\varepsilon_{w}}\,\lambda_{\max,+}^{1/2} \bigg(\sum_{i\in I} (\boldsymbol w_{| I})_i (\boldsymbol\Sigma - \boldsymbol\zeta_i\boldsymbol\zeta_i^\top)\bigg) + (1+\sqrt{2\varepsilon_{w}}) \|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|I}}\|_2. \end{align} Furthermore, as already mentioned earlier, for every $\boldsymbol w\in\mathcal W_n (\varepsilon)$, $\varepsilon_w\le \varepsilon/(1-\varepsilon)\le 1.5\varepsilon$. This implies that \begin{align} \mathbf E^{1/2}[\Xi^2] &\le 3\varepsilon + (1+\sqrt{3\varepsilon}) \mathbf E^{1/2}\bigg[\sup_{\boldsymbol w,I}\|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|I}}\|_2^2\bigg]\\ &\qquad + \sqrt{3\varepsilon}\,\mathbf E^{1/2}\bigg[\sup_{\boldsymbol w,I} \lambda_{\max,+}\bigg(\sum_{i\in I} (\boldsymbol w_{| I})_i (\boldsymbol\Sigma - \boldsymbol\zeta_i\boldsymbol\zeta_i^\top)\bigg) \bigg]. \end{align} As proved in \Cref{lemma2} (by taking $m=2o$ and $o=n\varepsilon$), \begin{align} \mathbf E^{1/2}\bigg[\sup_{\boldsymbol w,I}\|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|I}}\|_2^2\bigg] \le {\sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n}}\,\big(1+7\sqrt{\varepsilon}\big) + 9.2\varepsilon \sqrt{\log(2/\varepsilon)}. \end{align} In addition, in view of the first claim of \Cref{lemma3} (with $m=2o$ and $o=n\varepsilon$), stated and proved in the last section, we have \begin{align} \mathbf E\bigg[\sup_{\boldsymbol w,I} \lambda_{\max,+}\bigg(\sum_{i\in I} (\boldsymbol w_{| I})_i (\boldsymbol\Sigma - \boldsymbol\zeta_i\boldsymbol\zeta_i^\top)\bigg) \bigg] &\le 25\sqrt{p/n} + 66\varepsilon \log(1/2\varepsilon). \end{align} Combining \eqref{eq:14}, \eqref{eq:15} and \eqref{eq:16}, we get \begin{align} \mathbf E^{1/2}[\Xi^2] &\le 3\varepsilon + (1+\sqrt{3\varepsilon}) \big(\sqrt{p/n}\,\big(1+7\sqrt{\varepsilon}\big) + 9.2\varepsilon \sqrt{\log(2/\varepsilon)}\big)\\ &\qquad + \sqrt{3\varepsilon}\,\big(25\sqrt{p/n} + 66\varepsilon \log(1/2\varepsilon)\big)^{1/2}\\ &\le \sqrt{p/n}(1+16\sqrt{\varepsilon}) + 18\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(2/\varepsilon)} + \sqrt{3\varepsilon}\,\big(25\sqrt{p/n} + 66\varepsilon \log(1/2\varepsilon)\big)^{1/2}. \end{align} This leads to \eqref{ineq:xi2}. To obtain \eqref{ineq:xi1}, we repeat the same arguments but use the second claim of \Cref{lemma3} instead of the first one.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3
nodes.statement: We recall that, for any subset $I$ of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, \begin{align} R(\boldsymbol\zeta,\boldsymbol w, I) &= 2\varepsilon_{w}+\sqrt{2\varepsilon_{w}}\,\lambda_{\max,+}^{1/2} \bigg(\sum_{i\in I} (\boldsymbol w_{| I})_i (\boldsymbol\Sigma - \boldsymbol\zeta_i\boldsymbol\zeta_i^\top)\bigg) + (1+\sqrt{2\varepsilon_{w}}) \|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|I}}\|_2. \end{align} Furthermore, for every $\boldsymbol w\in\mathcal W_n (\varepsilon)$, $\varepsilon_w\le \varepsilon/(1-\varepsilon)\le 1.5\varepsilon$. This implies that \begin{align} \Xi &\le 3\varepsilon + \sqrt{3\varepsilon}\,\sup_{\boldsymbol w,I} \lambda_{\max,+}\bigg(\sum_{i\in I} (\boldsymbol w_{| I})_i (\boldsymbol\Sigma - \boldsymbol\zeta_i\boldsymbol\zeta_i^\top)\bigg)^{1/2} + (1+\sqrt{3\varepsilon}) \sup_{\boldsymbol w,I}\|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|I}}\|_2, \end{align} where $\sup_{\boldsymbol w,I}$ is the supremum over all $\boldsymbol w\in\mathcal W_n(\varepsilon)$ and over all $I\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}$ of cardinality larger than or equal to $n(1-\varepsilon)$. As proved in \Cref{lemma2bis} (by taking $m=2o$ and $o=n\varepsilon$), with probability at least $1-2e^{-t}$, \begin{align} \sup_{\boldsymbol w,I}\|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w_{|I}}\|_2 \le 16\sqrt{\frac{\tau p}{n}} + 13\varepsilon\sqrt{\tau\log(2/\varepsilon)} + 8\sqrt{\frac{2t\tau}{n}}. \end{align} In addition, in view of \Cref{lemma3:bis} (with $m=2o$ and $o=n\varepsilon$), with probability at least $1-2e^{-t}$, we have \begin{align} \sup_{\boldsymbol w,I}\lambda_{\max,+}\bigg(\sum_{i\in I} (\boldsymbol w_{| I})_i (\boldsymbol\Sigma - \boldsymbol\zeta_i\boldsymbol\zeta_i^\top)\bigg) &\le 5A_3 \bigg( \sqrt{ \frac{p+t}{n}} + \frac{p + t}{n} + 2\varepsilon\log(2/\varepsilon)\bigg)\\ &\le 13 A_3 \bigg( \sqrt{\frac{p + t}{n}} + \varepsilon\log(2/\varepsilon)\bigg), \end{align} where in the last inequality we have used that $p\le n$ and $t\le n$. Combining \eqref{eq:14b}, \eqref{eq:15b} and \eqref{eq:16b}, we obtain that the inequality \begin{align} \Xi &\le A_4\bigg(\sqrt{\frac{p + t}{n}} + \varepsilon \sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\bigg) \end{align} hold true with probability at least $1-4e^{-t}$, for every $t\in[0,n]$, where $A_4$ is a constant depending only on the variance proxy $\tau$. Replacing $t$ by $\log(4/\delta)$, we get the claim of the proposition.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: The first step of the proof consists in establishing a recurrent inequality relating the estimation error of $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k}$ to that of $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}$. More precisely, we show that this error decreases at a geometric rate, up to a small additive error term. Without loss of generality, we assume that $\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|_{\textup{op}} = 1$. Let us recall the notation \begin{align} \mathcal W_n(\varepsilon) = \Big\{\boldsymbol w\in \boldsymbol\Delta^{n-1}: \max_i w_i\le \frac1{n(1-\varepsilon)}\Big\} \end{align} and \begin{align} R(\boldsymbol\zeta,\boldsymbol w,I) = 2\varepsilon_w + \sqrt{2\varepsilon_w} \lambda^{1/2}_{\max,+}\bigg(\sum_{i\in I} ( \boldsymbol w_{|I})_i(\boldsymbol\Sigma - \boldsymbol\zeta_i\boldsymbol\zeta_i^\top)\bigg) +(1+\sqrt{2\varepsilon_w})\|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w|I}\|_2. \end{align} For every $k\ge 1$, in view of \Cref{proposition1} and \eqref{eq:minG}, we have \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 &\le \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon_k}}{ 1-\varepsilon_k} G(\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k})^{1/2} + \Xi\\ &\le \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon_k}}{ 1-\varepsilon_k} G(\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{1/2} + \Xi, \end{align} where \begin{align} \varepsilon_k = \sum_{i\not\in\mathcal I} w_i^{k}\le \frac{\varepsilon n }{n-n\varepsilon} = \frac{\varepsilon}{1- \varepsilon} \end{align} and \begin{align} \Xi = \max_{|I|\ge n-n\varepsilon} \sup_{\boldsymbol w\in \mathcal W_n (\varepsilon)} R(\boldsymbol\zeta,\boldsymbol w,I). \end{align} Inequality \eqref{epsk} and the cat that the function $x\mapsto \sqrt{x}/(1-x)$ is increasing for $x\in[0,1)$ imply that \begin{align} \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon_k}}{ 1-\varepsilon_k} \le \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}}{ 1-2\varepsilon} = \alpha_\varepsilon. \end{align} Using this inequality and the fact that $\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k$ is a minimizer of $G(\cdot, \widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})$, we infer from \eqref{mu:k} that \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_\varepsilon G(\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{1/2} + \Xi\\ &\le \alpha_\varepsilon G(\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I},\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{1/2} + \Xi, \end{align} where $\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}$ is the weight vector defined by $w^*_i = \mathds 1(i\in\mathcal I)/|\mathcal I|$. One can check that \begin{align} \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^* (\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{\otimes 2} &= \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^*(\boldsymbol X_i-\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}})^{\otimes 2} + (\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{\otimes 2}\\ &\preceq \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^*(\boldsymbol X_i-\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}})^{\otimes 2} + \big\|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\big\|_2^2\,\mathbf I_p\\ &\preceq \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^*(\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu^*)^{\otimes 2} + \big\|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\big\|_2^2\,\mathbf I_p. \end{align} This readily yields \begin{align} G(\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I},\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}) &\le \lambda_{\max,+} \bigg(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^*(\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu^*)^{\otimes 2} - \boldsymbol\Sigma\bigg) + \big\|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\big\|_2^2\\ &\le G(\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}, \boldsymbol\mu^*) + \big(\big\|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}\big\|_2 + \big\|\boldsymbol\mu^*-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\big\|_2\big)^2. \end{align} Combining with inequality \eqref{mu:k1}, we arrive at \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_\varepsilon G(\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}, \boldsymbol\mu^*)^{1/2} + \alpha_\varepsilon\big\|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{ \boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}\big\|_2 + \alpha_\varepsilon \big\|\boldsymbol\mu^*-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\big\|_2 + \Xi. \end{align} Thus, we have obtained the desired recurrent inequality \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_\varepsilon \big\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\big\|_2 +\widetilde\Xi, \end{align} with \begin{align} \widetilde\Xi &= \alpha_\varepsilon G(\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}, \boldsymbol\mu^*)^{1/2} + \alpha_\varepsilon\big\|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{ \boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}\big\|_2 + \Xi\\ &\le \sqrt{5\varepsilon}\,\sup_{\boldsymbol w,I} \bigg\|\sum_{i\in I} (\boldsymbol w_{| I})_i (\boldsymbol\Sigma - \boldsymbol\zeta_i\boldsymbol\zeta_i^\top)\bigg\|_{\rm op}^{1/2} + \sqrt{5\varepsilon}\,\big\|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{ \boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}\big\|_2 + \Xi. \end{align} The last inequality above follows from the inequality $\alpha_\varepsilon\le \sqrt{5\varepsilon}$ as soon as $\varepsilon\le 0.3$. Unfolding the recurrent inequality \eqref{mu:k3}, we get \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{K}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_\varepsilon^K \big\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{0}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\big\|_2 +\frac{\widetilde\Xi}{1-\alpha_\varepsilon}. \end{align} In view of \Cref{lemma0} and the condition $\varepsilon \le 0.3$, we get \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{K}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 &\le \frac{5\alpha_\varepsilon^K}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \big\|\boldsymbol\zeta_i\big\|_2 +\frac{\widetilde\Xi}{1-\alpha_\varepsilon}. \end{align} Simple algebra yields \begin{align} \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \big\|\boldsymbol\zeta_i\big\|_2 &\le \bigg(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \big\|\boldsymbol\xi_i\big\|_2^2\bigg)^{1/2} \le \sqrt{p} + \bigg(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (\big\|\boldsymbol\xi_i\big\|_2^2-p)\bigg)^{1/2}\\ &= \sqrt{p} + \bigg(\frac{\mathop{\textup{Tr}}(\boldsymbol\xi_{1:n}\boldsymbol\xi_{1:n}^\top -\mathbf I_p)}n\bigg)^{1/2}\\ &\le \sqrt{p} + \sqrt{p/n}\,\big\|\boldsymbol\xi_{1:n}\boldsymbol\xi_{1:n}^\top -\mathbf I_p\big\|_{\rm op}^{1/2}. \end{align} Thus, in view of \Cref{lem:smaxbis}, with probability at least $1-\delta$, \begin{align} \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \big\|\boldsymbol\zeta_i\big\|_2 &\le \sqrt{p}\bigg(1 +\sqrt{2A_3} + \sqrt{\frac{1.5 A_3\log(1/\delta)}{n}}\bigg). \end{align} Since $\delta\ge 4e^{-n}$ and $K$ is chosen in such a way that $\alpha_\varepsilon^K \le 0.5\varepsilon/\sqrt{p}$, we get, on an event of probability at least $1-\delta$, \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{K}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 &\le 0.5 \varepsilon(1+3A_3) +\frac{\widetilde\Xi}{1-\alpha_\varepsilon}. \end{align} Combining \eqref{xi:tilde} with \Cref{proposition3}, \Cref{lem:9} and \Cref{lemma3:bis}, we check that for some constant $A_5$ depending only on the variance proxy $\tau$, the inequality \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{K}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 &\le \frac{A_5}{1-\alpha_\varepsilon} \Bigg(\sqrt{\frac{p+\log(4/\delta)}{n}} + \varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\Bigg) \end{align} holds with probability at least $1-4\delta$. This completes the proof of the theorem.
nodes.section: A High-probability bounds in the sub-Gaussian case
nodes.statement_short: Establish the contraction $\|\mu^k-\mu^*\|\le\alpha_\varepsilon\|\mu^{k-1}-\mu^*\|+\tilde\Xi$ and unfold it. The remainder $\tilde\Xi$ is bounded with high probability via Proposition 3 and Lemmas 8 and 13.

nodes.name: Plan and normalization
nodes.statement: The first step of the proof consists in establishing a recurrent inequality relating the estimation error of $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k}$ to that of $\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}$. More precisely, we show that this error decreases at a geometric rate, up to a small additive error term. Without loss of generality, we assume that $\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|_{\textup{op}} = 1$.
nodes.section: A High-probability bounds in the sub-Gaussian case
nodes.statement_short: Plan: prove a geometric contraction; WLOG $\|\Sigma\|_{op}=1$.

nodes.name: Recall notation
nodes.statement: Let us recall the notation \begin{align} \mathcal W_n(\varepsilon) = \Big\{\boldsymbol w\in \boldsymbol\Delta^{n-1}: \max_i w_i\le \frac1{n(1-\varepsilon)}\Big\} \end{align} and \begin{align} R(\boldsymbol\zeta,\boldsymbol w,I) = 2\varepsilon_w + \sqrt{2\varepsilon_w} \lambda^{1/2}_{\max,+}\bigg(\sum_{i\in I} ( \boldsymbol w_{|I})_i(\boldsymbol\Sigma - \boldsymbol\zeta_i\boldsymbol\zeta_i^\top)\bigg) +(1+\sqrt{2\varepsilon_w})\|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w|I}\|_2. \end{align}
nodes.section: A High-probability bounds in the sub-Gaussian case
nodes.statement_short: Recall $\mathcal W_n(\varepsilon)$ and $R$.

nodes.name: Equation (223)

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 1
nodes.statement: For every $k\ge 1$, in view of \Cref{proposition1} and \eqref{eq:minG}, we have \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 &\le \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon_k}}{ 1-\varepsilon_k} G(\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k})^{1/2} + \Xi\\ &\le \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon_k}}{ 1-\varepsilon_k} G(\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{1/2} + \Xi, \end{align} where \begin{align} \varepsilon_k = \sum_{i\not\in\mathcal I} w_i^{k}\le \frac{\varepsilon n }{n-n\varepsilon} = \frac{\varepsilon}{1- \varepsilon} \end{align} and \begin{align} \Xi = \max_{|I|\ge n-n\varepsilon} \sup_{\boldsymbol w\in \mathcal W_n (\varepsilon)} R(\boldsymbol\zeta,\boldsymbol w,I). \end{align}

nodes.statement_short: Proposition 1 and (eq:minG) bound the $k$-th error.

nodes.name: Bound $G(w^*,\mu^{k-1})$
nodes.statement: One can check that \begin{align} \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^* (\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{\otimes 2} &= \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^*(\boldsymbol X_i-\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}})^{\otimes 2} + (\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{\otimes 2}\\ &\preceq \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^*(\boldsymbol X_i-\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}})^{\otimes 2} + \big\|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\big\|_2^2\,\mathbf I_p\\ &\preceq \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^*(\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu^*)^{\otimes 2} + \big\|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\big\|_2^2\,\mathbf I_p. \end{align} This readily yields \begin{align} G(\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I},\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}) &\le \lambda_{\max,+} \bigg(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^*(\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu^*)^{\otimes 2} - \boldsymbol\Sigma\bigg) + \big\|\bar{\boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\big\|_2^2\\ &\le G(\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}, \boldsymbol\mu^*) + \big(\big\|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}\big\|_2 + \big\|\boldsymbol\mu^*-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\big\|_2\big)^2. \end{align}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: This section provides a proof of \Cref{th:3}. Let $\varepsilon$ be the true contamination rate, which means that the distribution $\mathbf P\!_n\in\textup{SGAC}(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma, \varepsilon)$. Let $\ell^*$ be the largest value of $\ell$ such that the corresponding element $\varepsilon_\ell$ of the grid is larger than or equal to $\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon$ is assumed to be smaller than $\varepsilon_0 a$, the following inequalities hold \begin{align} \varepsilon_0 > \varepsilon_{\ell^*} \ge \varepsilon \ge \varepsilon_{\ell^*}a. \end{align} Let us introduce the events $\Omega_j = \{\boldsymbol\mu^*\in\mathbb B (\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}(\varepsilon_j),R_\delta( \varepsilon_j))\}$. Since $\mathbf P\!_n\in \textup{SGAC}(\boldsymbol\mu^*, \boldsymbol\Sigma,\varepsilon)\subseteq \textup{SGAC}(\boldsymbol\mu^*,\boldsymbol\Sigma, \varepsilon_j)$ for all $j \le \ell^*$. We infer from \Cref{th:2} that $\mathbf P (\Omega_j)\ge 1-4\delta/ \ell_{\max}$ for every $j\le \ell^*$. Hence, by the union bound, with probability at least $1-4\delta$, we have \begin{align} \boldsymbol\mu^*\in \bigcap_{j=1}^{\ell_*} \mathbb B \big(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}(\varepsilon_j),R_\delta( \varepsilon_j)\big). \end{align} From now on, we assume that this event is realized. Clearly, this implies that $\widehat\ell\ge \ell^*$ and, therefore, \begin{align} \mathbb B \big(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}}(\varepsilon_{\ell^*}),R_\delta( \varepsilon_{\ell^*})\big) \cap \mathbb B \big(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{AIR}},R_\delta( \varepsilon_{\widehat\ell})\big)\neq \varnothing\qquad \text{and}\qquad \varepsilon_{\widehat\ell}\le \varepsilon_{\ell^*}. \end{align} Using the triangle inequality, we get \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{AIR}} - \widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}} (\varepsilon_{\ell^*})\|_2 \le R_\delta(\varepsilon_{\ell^*}) + 2R_\delta (\varepsilon_{\widehat\ell}) \le 2R_\delta (\varepsilon_{\ell^*}) \le 2R_\delta (\varepsilon/a), \end{align} where the last inequality follows from \eqref{chain:eps} and the fact that $z\mapsto R_\delta(z)$ is an increasing function. Combining \eqref{AIR:IR} and \eqref{ell*}, we get \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{AIR}} - \boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 \le \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{AIR}} - \widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}} (\varepsilon_{\ell^*})\|_2 + \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n^{\textup{IR}} (\varepsilon_{\ell^*})-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 \le 3R_\delta (\varepsilon/a). \end{align} This completes the proof of \Cref{th:3}.

nodes.statement_short: Lepski argument: on the event where all balls up to $\ell^*$ contain $\mu^*$ (Theorem 2 + union bound), the selected estimate is within $3R_\delta(\varepsilon/a)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: This section is devoted to the proof of \Cref{th:4}. We follow exactly the same steps as in the proof of \Cref{th:2}. Without loss of generality, we assume that $\|\boldsymbol\Sigma\|_{\textup{op}} \le 1$. For every $k\ge 1$, in view of \Cref{proposition1} and \eqref{eq:minG}, we have \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 &\le \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon_k}}{ 1-\varepsilon_k} G(\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k})^{1/2} + \Xi \le \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon_k}}{ 1-\varepsilon_k} G(\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{1/2} + \Xi, \end{align} where \begin{align} \varepsilon_k = \sum_{i\not\in\mathcal I} w_i^{k}\le \frac{\varepsilon n }{n-n\varepsilon} = \frac{\varepsilon} {1-\varepsilon} \end{align} and $\Xi = \max_{|I|\ge n-n\varepsilon} \sup_{\boldsymbol w\in \mathcal W_n(\varepsilon)} R(\boldsymbol\zeta,\boldsymbol w,I)$. Inequality \eqref{epskbis} and the cat that the function $x\mapsto \sqrt{x}/(1-x)$ is increasing for $x\in[0,1)$ imply that \begin{align} \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon_k}}{ 1-\varepsilon_k} \le \frac{\sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}}{ 1-2\varepsilon} = \alpha_\varepsilon. \end{align} Using this inequality and the obvious inequality $G(\boldsymbol w,\boldsymbol\mu)\le \|\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu)^{\otimes 2}\|^{1/2}_{\textup{op}}$, we infer from \eqref{mu:kbis} that \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_\varepsilon G(\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{1/2} + \Xi\\ &\le \alpha_\varepsilon \bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^n \widehat w_i^{k}(\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1} )^{\otimes 2}\bigg\|_{\textup{op}}^{1/2} + \Xi. \end{align} Then, using the fact that $\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k$ is the minimizer of $\boldsymbol w\mapsto\big\|\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1} )^{\otimes 2}\big\|_{\textup{op}}$, we get \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_\varepsilon G(\widehat{\boldsymbol w}^k,\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{1/2} + \Xi\\ &\le \alpha_\varepsilon\bigg\| \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^*(\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1})^{\otimes 2} \bigg\|_{\textup{op}}^{1/2} + \Xi, \end{align} where $\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}$ is the weight vector defined by $w^*_i = \mathds 1(i\in\mathcal I)/|\mathcal I|$. Simple algebra (see the proof of \Cref{th:2} for more details) yields \begin{align} \bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^*(\boldsymbol X_i-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1} )^{\otimes 2}\bigg\|_{\textup{op}}^{1/2} &\le \bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^*(\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu^*)^{\otimes 2}\bigg\|_{\textup{op}}^{1/2} + \big\|\bar{ \boldsymbol X}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\big\|_2\\ &\le\bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^*(\boldsymbol X_i-\boldsymbol\mu^*)^{\otimes 2} \bigg\|_{\textup{op}}^{1/2} + \big\|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}\big\|_2 + \big\|\boldsymbol\mu^*-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\big\|_2\\ &\le G(\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}, \boldsymbol\mu^*)^{1/2} + \|\boldsymbol\Sigma \|_{\textup{op}} +\big\|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{ \mathcal I}}\big\|_2 + \big\| \boldsymbol\mu^* - \widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1} \big\|_2. \end{align} Combining with inequality \eqref{mu:k1bis}, we arrive at \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_\varepsilon G(\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}, \boldsymbol\mu^*)^{1/2} + \alpha_\varepsilon + \alpha_\varepsilon\big\|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{ \boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}\big\|_2 + \alpha_\varepsilon \big\|\boldsymbol\mu^*-\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}\big\|_2 + \Xi. \end{align} Thus, we have obtained the desired recurrent inequality \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_\varepsilon \big\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{k-1}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\big\|_2 +\alpha_\varepsilon + \widetilde\Xi, \end{align} with \begin{align} \widetilde\Xi &= \alpha_\varepsilon G(\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}, \boldsymbol\mu^*)^{1/2} + \alpha_\varepsilon \big\|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{\boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}\big\|_2 + \Xi\\ &\le \sqrt{5\varepsilon}\,\sup_{\boldsymbol w,I}\bigg\|\sum_{i\in I} (\boldsymbol w_{| I})_i (\boldsymbol\Sigma - \boldsymbol\zeta_i\boldsymbol\zeta_i^\top) \bigg\|_{\rm op}^{1/2} + \sqrt{5\varepsilon}\,\big\|\bar{\boldsymbol\zeta}_{ \boldsymbol w^*_{\mathcal I}}\big\|_2 + \Xi. \end{align} The last inequality above follows from the inequality $\alpha_\varepsilon\le \sqrt{5\varepsilon}$ as soon as $\varepsilon\le 0.3$. Unfolding the recurrent inequality \eqref{mu:k3bis}, we get \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{K}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 &\le \alpha_\varepsilon^K \big\|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{0}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\big\|_2 +\frac{\alpha_\varepsilon + \widetilde\Xi}{1-\alpha_\varepsilon}. \end{align} In view of \Cref{lemma0} and the condition $\varepsilon \le 0.3$, we get \begin{align} \|\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{K}-\boldsymbol\mu^*\|_2 &\le \frac{5\alpha_\varepsilon^K}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \big\|\boldsymbol\zeta_i\big\|_2 +\frac{\alpha_\varepsilon +\widetilde\Xi}{1-\alpha_\varepsilon}. \end{align} We have already seen that with probability at least $1-4\delta$, \begin{align} \frac{5\alpha_\varepsilon^K}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \big\|\boldsymbol\zeta_i\big\|_2 +\frac{\widetilde\Xi}{1- \alpha_\varepsilon} \le \frac{A_5}{1-\alpha_\varepsilon} \Bigg(\sqrt{\frac{p+\log(4/\delta)}{n}} + \varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}\Bigg), \end{align} where $A_5>1$ is a constant depending only on $\tau$. In addition, we have $\alpha_\varepsilon \le \sqrt{ 5\varepsilon}$ and $\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)} \le 0.6 \sqrt{\varepsilon}$, which lead to $\alpha_\varepsilon + A_5\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/ \varepsilon)}\le 3A_5\sqrt{\varepsilon}$. This completes the proof of the theorem.

nodes.statement: There exist some universal constants $c, \widetilde{c} > 0$ such that if $n > \widetilde{c}$, then \begin{equation} \inf_{\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n} R_{\max}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n, \boldsymbol\Sigma, \varepsilon) \ge c \| \boldsymbol\Sigma \|_{\textup{op}}^{1/2} \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}{n}} + \varepsilon\bigg). \end{equation}
nodes.section: D Lower bound for the Gaussian model with adversarial contamination
nodes.origin_citation: Chen, Gao, Ren 2016, 2018 with Bateni & Dalalyan 2020, Prop. 1
nodes.statement_short: Any estimator has worst-case GAC risk $\gtrsim\|\Sigma\|^{1/2}(\sqrt{r_\Sigma/n}+\varepsilon)$.

nodes.name: Proof of the lower bound for GAC
nodes.statement: First, notice that it is sufficient to prove this bound for $\varepsilon > \sqrt{{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}/{n}}$. Indeed, if $\varepsilon < \sqrt{{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}/{n}}$ then one gets the desired lower bound by simply comparing GAC model with the standard outlier free model. More formally, \begin{align} \inf_{\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n} R_{\max}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n, \boldsymbol\Sigma, \varepsilon) \ge \inf_{\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n} R_{\max}^{\textup{OF}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n) = \sqrt{\frac{\mathop{\textup{Tr}}{\boldsymbol\Sigma}}{n}}, \end{align} where $R_{\max}^{\textup{OF}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n)$ is the worst case risk in the classical outlier free setting where the observations are i.i.d. and drawn from $\mathcal{N}_p(\boldsymbol\mu^*, \boldsymbol\Sigma)$. Since the GAC model is more general than HDC model, then one clearly has \begin{align} \inf_{\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n} R_{\max}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n, \boldsymbol\Sigma, \varepsilon) \ge \inf_{\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n} R_{\max}^{\textup{HDC}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n, \varepsilon). \end{align} On the other hand, in view of Eq. (4) from \citep{bateni2020minimax}, for every $r>0$, \begin{align} R_{\max}^{\textup{HDC}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n, \varepsilon) + r e^{-n\varepsilon/6} \ge \sup_{\mathbf P_n \in \mathcal{M}^{\textup{HC}}_n(0.5\varepsilon, \boldsymbol\mu^*)} r\mathbf{P} \big( \| \widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n - \boldsymbol\mu \|_2 \ge r\big). \end{align} Using the result of Theorem \ref{thm:lb-huber} and taking first $r = C \| \boldsymbol\Sigma\|_{\textup{op}}^{1/2}\big[\sqrt{{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}/{n}} + \varepsilon\big]$ then infimum of both sides one arrives at \begin{align} \inf_{\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n} R_{\max}^{\textup{HDC}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n, \varepsilon) \ge (C/4) \| \boldsymbol\Sigma\|_{\textup{op}}^{1/2}\bigg[\sqrt{\frac{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}{n}} + \varepsilon\bigg]\big(1 - 2e^{-n\varepsilon/6}\big). \end{align} Now, using $\varepsilon > \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}/n}$ one gets that $n\varepsilon > \sqrt{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma} n} \ge \sqrt{n}$. Therefore, taking $n \ge 36\log^2(4)$, one can check that \eqref{eq:lb-proof1} yields \begin{align} \inf_{\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n} R_{\max}^{\textup{HDC}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_n, 2\varepsilon) \ge (C/8) \| \boldsymbol\Sigma\|_{\textup{op}}^{1/2}\bigg[\sqrt{\frac{\textbf{\textup{r}}_{\scriptscriptstyle\boldsymbol\Sigma}}{n}} + \varepsilon\bigg]. \end{align} Then, the final result follows from \eqref{eq:ac-hdc} with constants $c = C/8$ and $\widetilde{c} = 36\log^2(4)$.

nodes.statement:
\qquad {Compute current weights:}\\
				
				\qquad\quad $\displaystyle	\boldsymbol w \in \mathop{\textup{arg\,min}}_{(n-n\varepsilon)\|\boldsymbol w\|_\infty\le 1}
